title: Claude for RFPs: How to Respond to RFPs with Claude Skills | Downloadable Skills + Detailed Guide Included
summary: A practical guide to using Claude for RFP responses: five custom Claude Skills, honest pros and cons, and the signals that you need a dedicated platform.
body_text: Proposal teams answered an average of 166 RFPs last year and spent about 25 hours on each one, according to Loopio's latest RFP Trends and Benchmarks research. Claude can read a 120-page RFP in under a minute and hand back a competent first draft before your coffee cools. Those two facts explain why "Claude for RFPs" keeps coming up in proposal team Slack channels. This guide takes the question seriously. It covers whether Claude belongs in your RFP process at all, the honest pros and cons, and a complete workflow built on five custom Claude Skills: a requirement extractor, a go/no-go analysis, a full RFP analysis, a responder, and a final proofreader. We build RFP response software at Inventive AI, so we watch this space closely and we will be upfront about our perspective. Claude is genuinely useful for some teams. This guide shows you how to get the most out of it, and where it runs out of road. Should You Use Claude for RFP Response Management? It depends on two numbers: how many RFPs you answer a year, and how many people touch each response. Claude works well when one person owns the process and volume stays low. If you respond to a handful of RFPs a year, your source material fits in a few dozen documents, and you personally review every answer before it ships, Claude will save you real time. It reads long, messy documents better than almost any general-purpose AI available today. Paid plans handle PDFs up to 1,000 pages and give you a 200K token context window, roughly 150,000 words of working memory. That covers most mid-sized RFPs plus your supporting material. The math changes as volume grows. Every new RFP means re-feeding Claude the same product specs, security posture, and pricing guardrails. Every question means a prompt, a review, a copy, and a paste. An RFP with 80 questions means running that loop 80 times, and the formatting is on you. When four or more collaborators need to review and approve answers, a chat window has no way to assign question 12 to Legal or track who signed off on question 45. Here is a reasonable line in the sand. Under 10 to 15 RFPs a year with one or two owners, Claude plus the skills in this guide will genuinely change your workload. Above that, the manual overhead starts eating what the drafting saves. Loopio found that 68% of proposal teams used generative AI in the past year, and the teams running at volume mostly pair a general AI assistant with purpose-built response software rather than picking one or the other. ‍ Pros and Cons of Using Claude for RFP Responses Where Claude genuinely shines Long-document comprehension. RFPs arrive as sprawling PDFs with appendices, amendment letters, and buried submission rules. Claude holds all of it in one context and reasons across the full package. This is its single biggest advantage over older AI tools that choked past 20 pages. Structured analysis. Ask for a compliance matrix, an evaluation criteria breakdown, or a gap analysis against your product docs and you get organized, usable output. The analysis is often more valuable than the prose. Claude Projects. A Project gives you a persistent workspace where your past proposals, product documentation, and boilerplate live across conversations. Set project instructions once and every chat inherits them. Claude Skills. Skills let you package your RFP workflow into reusable instructions that Claude applies automatically. This is the feature that turns Claude from a clever intern into something closer to a process. The entire third section of this guide is built on it. Cost. A paid Claude seat costs a small fraction of dedicated proposal software. For a team of one, that matters. Where it costs you Context needs constant babysitting. Claude does not know which product details apply to which customer. You feed it background for every new RFP, and when your product changes, you update the files yourself. Teams consistently report that this maintenance quietly consumes the hours the drafting saved. Old content never dies. Uploading new files to a Project does not retire the old ones. Claude has no concept of a single source of truth, so a deprecated spec from last year's proposal can surface in this year's answer. On a security questionnaire, that is a real liability. The copy-paste loop. Claude is a chat window. Each batch of questions goes in, each batch of answers comes out, and you carry every answer back into the issuer's template by hand. No workflow layer. There are no assignments, no reviewer routing, no approval states, no audit trail. Five people using Claude are five people with five separate contexts, and nobody knows which answer is final. It will guess unless you stop it. Claude fills gaps confidently. Without explicit instructions to cite sources and flag missing information, you will catch invented details late, or worse, after submission. Security review is on you. Consumer Claude plans include a model-training setting and data retention policies you should read before uploading confidential bid material. Enterprise agreements differ. Check first. None of these problems kill Claude at low volume. They compound at scale. Keep that pattern in mind as you build the workflow below. How to Use Claude for RFP Response Management with Claude Skills Claude Skills are the difference between prompting from scratch every time and running a repeatable process. A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file inside: instructions, output formats, and reference files that Claude loads automatically whenever a task matches the Skill's description. You write the workflow once. Claude applies it every time. Two prerequisites. Custom Skills require a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) with code execution enabled. To install one, open the Skills section in Claude's settings, choose Create skill, and upload your Skill folder as a ZIP file. ‍ Step 1: Build your project knowledge base Before any Skill runs, create a Claude Project for RFP work and upload: Three to five recent winning proposals Current product and security documentation Approved boilerplate: company overview, implementation methodology, support tiers Pricing guardrails, meaning what you can and cannot commit to A short tone guide, or a few answers you consider the gold standard Then set the project instructions: answer only from the uploaded files, name the source document for every claim, and write "Information unavailable" when the files do not cover a question. These three rules prevent most hallucination problems before they start. Keep the folder clean. Every stale file in your Project is a wrong answer waiting to happen. Skill 1: Requirement Extractor Miss one mandatory requirement and the rest of your proposal may never be read. This Skill reads the full RFP package and produces a numbered requirements table you can use as a compliance matrix. One caution from experience: spot-check the output against the original document, especially appendices and dense tables. Claude is good at this task. It is not perfect, and a missed "shall" is expensive. You are helping me build a custom Claude Skill. Generate the complete contents of a SKILL.md file for a skill named "rfp-requirement-extractor" . The YAML front matter must contain a name field and a description field. The description should tell Claude to use this skill whenever a user uploads an RFP, RFI, or questionnaire and asks for requirements, a compliance matrix, or extraction. The skill instructions must tell Claude to: 1. Read every page of the attached RFP, including appendices, footnotes, amendment letters, and embedded tables. 2. Extract every requirement into a table with these columns: ID | Requirement (verbatim) | Source section | Type | Suggested owner | Status 3. Quote requirement text verbatim, never paraphrase. 4. Classify Type as Mandatory, Optional, or Informational. Treat "shall" and "must" as Mandatory in every case . 5. Include submission requirements (format, deadline, page limits, required forms, certifications) as their own rows. 6. End with a count of total requirements found, broken down by type, plus a list of any sections it could not fully parse so a human can check them. Output only the SKILL.md content in a single markdown code block. Skill 2: Go/No-Go Analysis The average RFP win rate sits around 45%, and the fastest way to raise yours is to stop chasing bids you were never going to win. This Skill scores each opportunity against your ideal customer profile before anyone spends a week writing. Give the Skill reference files that define your ICP, your disqualifiers, and your minimum deal economics. Then have it score the RFP on: Solution fit against the mandatory requirements Incumbent signals, such as requirements written suspiciously close to one vendor's spec sheet Timeline feasibility against your team's current load Compliance blockers you cannot meet Deal size against the effort a full response demands Output: a weighted score, a pursue-or-pass recommendation, and the three factors that drove it. Prompt: "Run go/no-go analysis on this RFP using our ICP criteria." The Skill is only as sharp as the criteria you give it. A vague ICP file produces a shrug with numbers attached. You are helping me build a custom Claude Skill. Generate the complete contents of a SKILL.md file for a skill named "rfp-go-no-go-analysis" . The YAML front matter must contain a name field and a description field. The description should tell Claude to use this skill when a user asks whether to pursue, bid, or pass on an RFP or opportunity. The skill instructions must tell Claude to: 1. Read the full RFP and compare it against our ideal customer profile: [DESCRIBE YOUR ICP: industry, company size, use cases, regions] 2. Apply our hard disqualifiers: [LIST DISQUALIFIERS, e.g. on-premise-only deployments, certifications we lack, unacceptable liability terms] 3. Respect our minimum deal economics: [e.g. estimated contract value must exceed $X, response effort must stay under Y person-days] 4. Score the opportunity from 0 to 100 across five weighted factors: solution fit against mandatory requirements ( 30 %), incumbent signals such as requirements written around one vendor 's spec sheet (20%), timeline feasibility (20%), compliance blockers (20%), deal size versus effort (10%). 5. Return the weighted score, a clear PURSUE or PASS recommendation, the three factors that drove the decision, and any assumptions it made due to missing information. Output only the SKILL.md content in a single markdown code block. Skill 3: Full RFP Analysis Once you decide to pursue, this Skill produces the brief your whole team reads before anyone writes a word. It digs out: Evaluation criteria and their weighting, stated or implied The buyer's priorities, including the ones between the lines Competitive hints, like spec'd-in features that suggest who else is bidding Red flags: vague scope, compressed timelines, unusual liability terms Submission logistics: deadline, format, page limits, required certifications and forms Ask it to end with the three themes your response should hammer. A response shaped around what the evaluator actually scores beats a generic feature tour every time. You are helping me build a custom Claude Skill. Generate the complete contents of a SKILL.md file for a skill named "rfp-full-analysis" . The YAML front matter must contain a name field and a description field. The description should tell Claude to use this skill when a user asks for a full analysis, briefing, or breakdown of an RFP they have decided to pursue. The skill instructions must tell Claude to produce a pre-writing brief with these sections: 1. Evaluation criteria and their weighting, both stated and implied. Where weighting is not stated, infer it from emphasis and section length and say so explicitly. 2. The buyer 's priorities, including unstated ones visible between the lines (repeated themes, pain points implied by requirements, political context). 3. Competitive hints: features or language that suggest which vendors shaped the requirements or are likely bidding. 4. Red flags: vague scope, compressed timelines, unusual liability or IP terms, budget signals that conflict with the scope. 5. Submission logistics: deadline, format, page limits, required forms and certifications, submission portal details. 6. A closing list of the three win themes our response should be built around, each tied to a specific evaluation criterion. Output only the SKILL.md content in a single markdown code block. Skill 4: Responder This is the drafting engine. The Skill instructs Claude to answer each question strictly from project knowledge, name the source document per answer, note its confidence, and flag anything the files do not cover instead of improvising. Work in batches of 10 to 20 questions rather than the whole document at once. Answer quality drifts on very long generations, and smaller batches keep your review manageable. Now the honest part. This is where the chat-window ceiling becomes physical. Every batch needs review, then copying, then re-formatting into the issuer's template, and an 80-question RFP means doing that dance all afternoon. Inventive AI was built around this exact gap: you upload the full RFP file, AI agents draft every answer with citations from governed company knowledge, and the export comes back in the issuer's original formatting. If the loop is your daily reality, book a 20-minute Inventive AI demo and watch a full RFP get drafted in one pass. You are helping me build a custom Claude Skill. Generate the complete contents of a SKILL.md file for a skill named "rfp-responder" . The YAML front matter must contain a name field and a description field. The description should tell Claude to use this skill when a user asks it to draft, answer, or respond to RFP or questionnaire questions. The skill instructions must tell Claude to: 1. Answer strictly from the project knowledge files. Never use general knowledge to fill gaps about our product, security posture, or pricing. 2. For every answer, output : the question number, the draft answer, the name of the source document the answer came from , and a confidence level of High, Medium, or Low. 3. Write "Information unavailable - needs SME input" instead of guessing whenever the files do not cover a question, and add the question to a gap list at the end of the batch. 4. Match our voice: [DESCRIBE TONE, e.g. plain, direct, confident, no superlatives, US spelling]. Follow the gold-standard answers in [REFERENCE FILE NAME] for length and structure. 5. Respect answer length limits when the question states one, and default to [X] words otherwise. 6. Work only on the batch of questions provided in the current message, and remind the user to review each batch before requesting the next. Output only the SKILL.md content in a single markdown code block. Skill 5: Final Proofreader The last Skill runs before submission and checks the assembled document, not the chat history. It verifies that: Every requirement in the extractor's table has a corresponding response Product names, version numbers, and terminology stay consistent throughout Tone matches your voice guide from the project files No two sections contradict each other on pricing, timelines, or scope Word and page limits are respected Have it return a pass/fail list with exact locations instead of rewritten text. You want a findings report you can act on, with a human making every correction. You are helping me build a custom Claude Skill. Generate the complete contents of a SKILL.md file for a skill named "rfp-final-proofreader" . The YAML front matter must contain a name field and a description field. The description should tell Claude to use this skill when a user asks for a final check, proofread, or pre-submission review of an assembled RFP response. The skill instructions must tell Claude to check the attached assembled document (not the chat history) and verify that: 1. Every requirement in the attached compliance matrix has a corresponding response in the document , mapped by requirement ID. 2. Product names, version numbers, and terminology are consistent throughout. 3. Tone matches the voice guide in the project files. 4. No two sections contradict each other on pricing, timelines, scope, or commitments. 5. Stated word, page, and format limits are respected. 6. All placeholder text, internal comments, and draft markers are removed. The skill must return a findings report, never a rewritten document : a pass/fail line per check, and for every failure the exact location (section heading and quoted sentence) plus a one-line description of the problem, so a human makes every correction. Output only the SKILL.md content in a single markdown code block. Five Best Practices That Keep Claude Honest on RFPs Make citations mandatory. Every answer names its source document. This one rule catches most hallucinations at review time instead of after submission, because an answer with no source is a guess wearing a suit. Replace files, never accumulate them. When product docs change, delete the old version from your Project the same day you upload the new one. Claude treats everything in context as equally true, and a quarterly purge is cheaper than one wrong security answer. The habits in our guide to building a competitive RFP answer library apply directly to Claude Projects. Batch by section. Feed the responder 10 to 20 questions at a time, grouped by topic. You get better answers, and your SME reviewers can work in parallel on different sections. Keep a human gate on every answer. AI drafts, subject-matter experts verify, someone accountable approves. Issuers increasingly ask whether AI was used in a response, and some require disclosure. A real review gate means you can answer that question comfortably. Check your data settings before the first upload. Confirm the model-training setting is off, understand the retention policy on your plan, and check your customer contracts for confidentiality clauses that cover sharing bid material with third-party services. Five minutes of reading beats one awkward conversation with Legal. When Claude Stops Being Enough Watch for these signals: You answer more than 10 to 15 RFPs a year and the context babysitting has become someone's part-time job Four or more people review each response and version control lives in a Slack thread Your product changes faster than your Project folder, and stale answers keep slipping through Security questionnaires arrive as rigid multi-tab Excel workbooks that a chat window cannot fill or export cleanly A prospect or auditor asks who approved an answer, and you have no record Two or three of these at once means the chat window is now the bottleneck. The drafting was never the hard part. The process around it is. How Inventive AI Handles RFP Response Management Inventive AI is an agentic RFP response platform built for exactly the workflow this guide assembles by hand. You upload the full RFP in PDF, Word, Excel, or PowerPoint. AI agents extract the questions, pull the right context per question from a Knowledge Hub connected to the systems you already use , and draft every answer with source citations and a confidence score. Your team reviews, refines, and approves in one shared workspace. What that replaces from this guide: Full-document intake instead of pasting question batches: extraction, drafting, and formatted export in one pass Knowledge Hub with live sync to SharePoint, Google Drive, Salesforce, Confluence, and Notion, so there is no separate library to babysit Content Governance Agent that flags conflicting, outdated, and duplicate content automatically, retiring the stale-file problem Citations and confidence scores on every answer , with "Information unavailable" instead of guessing Built-in Go/No-Go and Full Response Analyzer agents , the same analysis Skills above, run automatically Assignments, reviewer workflows, and approvals with progress tracking across every active RFP, RFI, DDQ, and security questionnaire SOC 2 Type II compliance , and customer data is never used to train public models The results hold up in production. Insider cut response time by 90% and lifted its win rate from 30% to 50%. AssetWorks Facilities measured a 422% ROI with $105K in net savings . MaxVal completed 80 RFP questions in 3 hours, work that used to take most of a week. If your team has outgrown the copy-paste loop, book a demo with Inventive AI and bring the most difficult RFP you have. ‍ FAQs Is it safe to upload confidential RFP documents to Claude? It depends on your plan and settings. On consumer plans, check whether the model-training setting is enabled and review the data retention policy before uploading anything sensitive. Team and Enterprise agreements carry different terms, so read yours. Also check the RFP itself: many issuers include confidentiality clauses that restrict sharing bid material with third-party services. Purpose-built RFP platforms typically address this with SOC 2 compliance and contractual no-training commitments. Can Claude fill out an Excel questionnaire directly? Claude can read Excel files and draft answers to the questions inside them. It struggles with complex workbooks that use multiple tabs, merged cells, or hidden rows, and it cannot reliably write answers back into a rigid template without breaking the formatting. For SIG, CAIQ, and similar structured questionnaires, expect to re-enter answers manually. Is Claude better than ChatGPT for RFP responses? Claude's advantages are long-document handling and writing quality: a 200K token context on paid plans and support for PDFs up to 1,000 pages. ChatGPT counters with its own ecosystem of tools. For RFP work specifically, the gaps are identical in both: no governed content library, no approval workflow, and a per-question loop. Choose either for drafting. Neither one manages the process. Do we have to disclose that we used AI in an RFP response? Read the submission instructions. Some issuers, particularly in government procurement, now ask directly whether AI was used and how. Whatever the requirement, run every answer through human review and approval so you can stand behind the final document as your own work. How many RFP questions can Claude handle in one go? The context window can hold an entire RFP, but answer quality drifts on very long generations. Batches of 10 to 20 questions produce noticeably better drafts than a single 80-question run. Re-run weak answers individually with extra context rather than regenerating the whole batch. ‍ ‍

body_text: A popular Bubble Skincare sunscreen pack has been stopped at the UK border after regulators identified issues with its cosmetic labelling and product traceability requirements. The Bubble Cosmetics Sunscreen Pack was classified as a high-risk product by the UK Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS). According to the regulator's notice, the imported pack did not meet several mandatory requirements under the UK's applicable cosmetics rules. The action has raised questions about what the decision means for consumers who may have purchased individual Bubble sunscreen products in the UK. Why Was the Bubble Sunscreen Pack Stopped? The OPSS identified concerns involving the information supplied with the sunscreen products. In particular, the pack did not provide adequate instructions explaining best practice for using the sunscreen. Sunscreen is a product where clear usage information is particularly important. Consumers need to understand how much product to apply, how often it should be reapplied and how it should be used alongside other sun protection measures. Regulators also identified problems with product traceability. Traceability information allows authorities to identify and follow a cosmetic product through the supply chain, helping them respond effectively if a safety or compliance issue arises. The OPSS therefore determined that multiple mandatory cosmetic labelling requirements had not been satisfied. What Products Were Included? The affected Bubble Cosmetics Sunscreen Pack contained three products designed to provide mineral sun protection. These included a Tinted Daily Mineral Sunscreen, a Mineral Sunscreen Stick and Bubble Skincare Solar Mate Mineral Sunscreen. The products in the pack were reported as having SPF ratings ranging from 30 to 40. The products are associated with Bubble Skincare, a brand known for skincare products aimed at younger consumers and people looking for modern, lightweight formulations. Individual Bubble sunscreen products have also been sold through UK retailers, including Boots. Prices for the products were reported to range from approximately £14 to £19 individually. However, the specific sunscreen pack that was stopped at the UK border cannot be sold in the UK as a result of the regulatory action. Does This Mean All Bubble Sunscreen Is Banned? Not necessarily. The regulatory action relates specifically to the Bubble Cosmetics Sunscreen Pack identified in the OPSS notice. Consumers should not automatically assume that every Bubble sunscreen product available in the UK has been banned or declared unsafe. The issue described by the regulator concerns compliance with cosmetic labelling and traceability requirements. That is different from a finding that the sunscreen ingredients themselves are dangerous. This distinction is important because a product can be stopped from entering a market because its packaging, instructions or traceability information does not meet legal requirements. Consumers who own a Bubble sunscreen product should therefore check the exact product name, packaging and batch information rather than assuming that the regulatory notice applies to every Bubble item. What Does "High Risk" Mean? The term "high risk" can sound alarming, but it should be understood in the context of product safety enforcement. In this case, the regulator's concerns included missing or inadequate information required for consumers to use the product appropriately, as well as weaknesses in traceability. Proper cosmetic labelling is an important part of consumer protection. Labels can provide essential details about how a product should be used, who is responsible for placing it on the market and how the product can be identified if regulators need to investigate it. For sunscreen, instructions are particularly relevant because incorrect application can reduce the level of protection consumers expect from the SPF stated on the packaging. What Should Consumers Do? If you have a Bubble sunscreen product, start by checking exactly which product you have and where it was purchased. If it is part of the specific sunscreen pack identified in the regulatory notice, consumers should pay close attention to any guidance issued by the retailer, manufacturer or relevant UK authorities. It is also sensible to check the product packaging for usage instructions and traceability information. If important information appears to be missing, consumers can contact the retailer or manufacturer for clarification. When using sunscreen generally, follow the instructions provided on the product and do not rely on sunscreen alone. Seeking shade, wearing protective clothing and avoiding prolonged exposure to intense sunlight are also important parts of sun protection. Why Sunscreen Labelling Matters Sunscreen products are designed to protect skin from ultraviolet radiation, but their effectiveness depends partly on correct use. A product labelled with an SPF rating must be used according to its instructions to provide the intended level of protection. Applying too little sunscreen, failing to reapply it or overlooking areas of exposed skin can all reduce protection. That is why regulatory requirements surrounding instructions, warnings and traceability are more than a packaging issue. They help consumers make informed decisions and give regulators the information they need to monitor products in the marketplace. What Happens Next? The border action means the identified Bubble Cosmetics Sunscreen Pack cannot be sold in the UK. The OPSS notice highlights the importance of meeting the UK's cosmetic requirements before products enter the market. For consumers, the key point is that the action concerns a specific product pack and identified compliance issues. Anyone concerned about a particular Bubble sunscreen should check the exact product details rather than relying on headlines or social media posts. Source: The Sun on 19 August 2026.

summary: FOSTER CITY, Calif., Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Sagimet Biosciences Inc. body_text: FOSTER CITY, Calif., Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Sagimet Biosciences Inc. (Nasdaq: SGMT), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing novel therapeutics targeting dysfunctional metabolic and fibrotic pathways, today announced that, in connection with the hiring of 3 employees, the Compensation Committee of Sagimet’s Board of Directors approved that an inducement grant of 260,700 stock options in aggregate to purchase shares of the Company’s Series A common stock be granted on August 17, 2026 to the newly hired employees. The option awards were granted pursuant to the Nasdaq Rule 5635(c)(4) inducement grant exception as a component of each individual’s employment compensation and were granted as an inducement material to the acceptance of employment with Sagimet. The options have an exercise price equal to the closing price of Sagimet’s Series A common stock as reported by the Nasdaq Global Market on August 17, 2026. The options have a ten-year term and vest over four years, with 25% of the number of shares underlying each stock option vesting on the one-year anniversary of the applicable vesting commencement date (based on the employee’s employment commencement date) and the remaining shares vesting monthly over 36 months thereafter, subject to each individual’s continued service with Sagimet through the applicable vesting dates. About Sagimet Biosciences Sagimet is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing novel FASN inhibitors designed to target dysfunctional metabolic and fibrotic pathways in conditions resulting from the overproduction of the fatty acid, palmitate. FASN is a regulator of lipid synthesis, and a key pathway implicated in multiple diseases, such as acne, MASH and certain FASN-dependent tumor types. For additional information about Sagimet, please visit www.sagimet.com . Investor Contact: Joyce Allaire LifeSci Advisors JAllaire@LifeSciAdvisors.com Media Contact: Maggie Whitney LifeSci Communications mwhitney@lifescicomms.com

title: Content Marketing World 2026: Attendee travel guide
summary: Plan Colorado Convention Center hotels, DEN airport transit, GSA budget, Expo Hall strategy, summits, and how to make three days count at mile-high altitude.
body_text: But how you plan your week in Denver overall — lodging within walking distance, summit blocks on your calendar, and Expo Hall time protected from back-to-back breakouts — can shape whether you return with a sharper content roadmap and vendor short list or a folder of unread session slides and an expense report you keep postponing. A well-planned mile-high week can leave you with clearer measurement frameworks, stronger creator relationships, and next-quarter campaign ideas. What is Content Marketing World, and who is it for? Content Marketing World is the flagship content marketing conference hosted by the Content Marketing Institute and Informa, bringing strategists, creators, and insights leaders together for keynotes, breakouts, workshops, and the Expo Hall.[1] The 2026 edition runs Monday, Oct. 5 through Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at the Colorado Convention Center in downtown Denver, with optional pre-programming for first-time attendees on Sunday, Oct. 4.[1][2] The program packs 100+ sessions under the Insight to Impact theme, with Gabrielle Union announced as a keynote speaker and co-located programming from TMRE (The Market Research Event) and LIONS brands including Effie, WARC, and Contagious.[1][3] Informa lists 3,000+ attendees for the flagship event.[1] The crowd blends content strategists building editorial calendars, brand marketers evaluating martech stacks, SEO and social leads chasing discoverability wins, and insights directors who need customer research to inform creative. If you're pitching the trip internally, frame ROI around shortlisting martech before renewal season, earning the AI in Action Summit certification, or finishing a scored Expo Hall vendor walkthrough. What makes Content Marketing World 2026 worth the trip Content Marketing World compresses months of content-strategy research into three days of keynotes, summits, and Expo Hall demos — established category leaders next to emerging creators, with practitioners sharing what actually moved engagement and pipeline.[1] For strategists, that means tracks on AI in marketing, measurement frameworks, and storytelling you can't replicate from a webinar. For leaders, it means the Marketing Effectiveness Summit and Extra Innings Party, where relationships with agencies and martech partners actually deepen. Plan time for programming that happens on the floor and after hours, not only in session rooms: Science & Magic Summit (Monday): WARC and Contagious programming on cultural trends reshaping marketing — All Access Pass holders[2] Marketing Effectiveness Summit (Tuesday): Effie-led sessions on insight, strategy, and measurable outcomes — All Access Pass holders[2] Extra Innings Party at Coors Field (Tuesday evening): Official evening event with food, music, and attendee networking[2] AI in Action Summit (Wednesday): Workshops and interactive sessions with certification — All Access and 3-Day Pass holders[2] Expo Hall Reception (Monday evening): Light bites, drinks, and martech conversations on the show floor[2] Community Meetup (Wednesday evening): Relaxed gathering before departure[2] Co-located TMRE: Customer insights programming for colleagues who lead research — cross-event group discounts for teams of three or more[3][4] The trip earns its worth when you return with a prioritized martech short list, an AI playbook leadership can share, or peer ties that carry into Q1 planning — not when post-trip logistics interfere with your goals. Where to stay for Content Marketing World 2026 Where you stay in Denver determines morning walk time to the Expo Hall, how easily you reset between martech demos, and whether the Extra Innings Party ends with a short walk home or a rideshare across downtown. The Colorado Convention Center sits at 700 14th Street in downtown Denver, and the Convention Center district puts you steps from the Expo Hall and summit rooms. Hotels by distance to Colorado Convention Center Match downtown neighborhoods by walk time, vibe, and typical October rates: Area Distance to venue Details Rates Convention Center district 0–5 minutes walking Hyatt Regency at Colorado Convention Center and adjacent downtown towers; shortest path to Expo Hall and official onPeak properties[5] Highest during conference week LoDo / Union Station 10–15 minutes walking Restaurants, breweries, and lighter evening vibe along 16th Street Mall and Larimer Square Moderate Capitol Hill / Uptown 15–20 minutes on foot or rideshare East-of-downtown residential blocks; quieter nights when CCC towers sell out Lower The Convention Center district minimizes friction for Monday keynotes and Tuesday summit programming. LoDo and Union Station trade a short walk for dinner options and a calmer evening feel after Coors Field. Capitol Hill and Uptown work when onPeak inventory is more limited — plan an extra 10 minutes each way or budget a quick rideshare during morning keynotes. Content Marketing World hotel pricing Content Marketing World's first Denver edition fills downtown hotels during October. Official housing runs through onPeak with limited availability — compare that block against open inventory before you commit.[5] During last October's downtown Denver conference week, the median nightly rate near the Colorado Convention Center was $343.[12] Stack that figure against your per-diem cap before you lock a Convention Center district block. Median hotel rate: Budget about $343 per night near the venue during October conference weeks — compare LoDo and Capitol Hill before you default to the closest tower.[12] Stay length: Business travelers averaged 2.6 nights, so price the trip as a multi-night stay anchored on Monday check-in and Thursday checkout, not a single conference night.[12] Check-in pattern: Monday check-in and Thursday checkout dominated recent downtown Denver bookings — land on Sunday, October 4 if you want the same pre-summit buffer most travelers used.[12] Late bookings: 44.1% of bookings landed within two weeks of check-in — if you're inside that window, compare remaining neighborhoods instead of waiting for rates to drop.[12] When to book: Two or more months ahead: Median near $343 per night — workable if your policy requires early approval, but not the cheapest window in recent downtown Denver data.[12] One to two months ahead: Median near $364 per night — the steepest window in this sample; consider avoiding non-refundable inventory here unless your travel policy requires it.[12] Two to four weeks ahead: Median near $354 per night — compare onPeak block rates against open LoDo inventory before you commit.[12] One to two weeks ahead: Median near $299 per night — the strategic window in recent downtown Denver data; book here when finance approval allows.[12] Last minute (under seven days): Median near $343 per night — inventory-dependent; scan Capitol Hill and Uptown alternatives rather than assuming last-minute savings.[12] Conference-week rates ran about 3% above a normal September week near the venue — a modest premium, but downtown blocks still fill up fast when multiple Informa events share the same halls.[12] Content Marketing World flight trends DEN is the main airport for Content Marketing World travelers. Navan flight data from the same October 2025 downtown Denver window shows 907 business flights into Denver, with 5.1% from international origins.[12] Most people flew from New York, Boston, San Francisco, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Newark.[12] East Coast and West Coast travelers benefit from a Sunday, Oct. 4 arrival when policy allows. You'll be better prepared for Monday Science & Magic Summit programming after a night to adjust to mile-high altitude — not after racing from DEN to downtown the same morning. Book your Content Marketing World trip with Navan Edge Navan Edge is a personal executive assistant for travel, powered by an agentic AI engine and 24/7 human travel experts, that lets you book flights, hotels, and restaurants from one conversation using your preferences and live inventory. For Content Marketing World week, you can ask it to compare convention-center towers against Lower Downtown and Capitol Hill properties for the amenities your team needs , then add your DEN flight without opening a second tab. See how to book a conference trip for the step-by-step workflow. When official onPeak blocks fill, Navan Edge can check for alternate options and neighborhoods in that same chat — no new thread. Human travel experts can enter the conversation if a multi-leg rebooking or anything else requires extra assistance. Get more value from your booking On Content Marketing World trips booked through Navan Edge, you can stack three reward layers on one reservation: hotel loyalty points and airline miles (as if you booked direct), credit card multipliers, and 5% back in Amazon Gift Cards on eligible hotel stays. The Loyalty Wallet keeps your program tiers visible so you can book the most rewarding option. See our guide on how to earn travel rewards on business trips for the full mechanics. Set your Denver budget before traveling Your pass price anchors the spreadsheet, but Content Marketing World week spending spans downtown lodging, DEN transfers, client dinners, and incidentals beyond Expo-provided hospitality. Federal per diem for Denver Federal per diem rates for Denver in October FY2027 break down as follows: $307 per day total: $215 lodging + $92 meals and incidental expenses (M&IE) M&IE breakdown: Breakfast $23, lunch $26, dinner $38, incidentals $5 — reduce your meal allowance for breakfasts, lunches, and Expo receptions Content Marketing World provides[6] Travel-day M&IE: First and last days on the road qualify for 75% reimbursement ($69)[6] The U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) publishes FY2027 rates in mid-August; re-check gsa.gov once those October Denver figures are posted before you submit expenses. October downtown lodging often clears the $215 federal cap by roughly $128 per night when medians sit near $343 — flag the gap with your approver before you commit, especially outside onPeak housing. Other expenses to consider All Access Advance: $2,749 through July 31, 2026; Standard All Access $2,949 (Aug. 1–Sept. 18) — verify current tiers at contentmarketingworld.com/registration before you register[7] 3-Day Pass Standard: $2,499; 2-Day Pass Standard: $2,099; Digital Pass Standard: $899 — confirm pass scope against summit and workshop access you need[7] Conference-provided meals: Expo Hall Reception and summit hospitality lower your meal allowance on days the event feeds you[2] Airport transfer: Regional Transportation District (RTD) A Line from DEN to Union Station about $10.50; rideshare typically $30–$50, higher with traffic[8][9] Client dinners: Downtown steakhouses and Larimer Square restaurants typically run $75–$150 per person After-hours networking: Extra Innings Party at Coors Field (included for qualifying passes) plus partner-hosted dinners — keep a small buffer beyond provided hospitality Sum registration, lodging, transfers, and networking buffers before you purchase, so finance sign-off and expense filing are straightforward. Plan your Content Marketing World agenda Content Marketing World's multi-track catalog, three co-located summits, and sprawling Expo Hall make over-scheduling a common mistake. Keep daily sessions to three or four and hold time for vendor demos, Coors Field networking, and hallway conversations. Public agenda at a glance Content Marketing World has published a day-by-day program structure on the official program overview — 100+ sessions across three main days plus optional Sunday pre-programming.[2] Sunday, Oct. 4: First-Time Attendees Welcome Session (4 p.m.) and Dinner with New Friends for solo travelers[2] Monday, Oct. 5: Keynotes and breakouts all day; Science & Magic Summit (All Access); Expo Hall Reception in the evening[2] Tuesday, Oct. 6: Keynotes and breakouts all day; Marketing Effectiveness Summit (All Access); Extra Innings Party at Coors Field in the evening[2] Wednesday, Oct. 7: Workshops and interactive sessions (3-Day and All Access passes); AI in Action Summit (All Access); Community Meetup in the evening[2] The full session scheduler with timed titles publishes closer to the event — star must-see tracks now using the program overview structure so you know which days require All Access versus 3-Day passes.[2] Build flexibility into your schedule Set aside half an hour before travel week for: Sessions: Flag must-see keynotes and breakout tracks once the scheduler opens; popular AI and measurement time slots fill up quickly.[2] Meetings: Email vendors, creators, or peers about two weeks out with a concrete 15-minute Expo or coffee slot. Logistics: Confirm onPeak housing reservation, download the CMI Events app, set out-of-office, and save Colorado Convention Center in your calendar.[5] Contacts: Choose QR, NFC, or LinkedIn — jot one reminder note per new contact while the conversation is still fresh. For flights, hotels, and departure checklists beyond this Content Marketing World list, see our business trip planning guide . What to pack and wear at Content Marketing World Content Marketing World calls for polished marketing casual: button-downs or blouses, slacks or dark denim, closed-toe shoes built for long Expo days, plus a blazer optional for keynotes or Larimer Square dinners. Agency teams often dress one notch sharper for the Extra Innings Party; creators and strategists lean toward smart casual with layers for long Expo days. Denver in early October runs mild in the afternoon — highs often in the upper 60s to low 70s°F — with cool evenings that can drop into the mid-40s°F and thin mile-high air that dries you out faster than coastal cities.[10] Layer up for air-conditioned breakout rooms, then peel off for sunny walks between the convention center and Larimer Square dinners. Conference essentials Rotating footwear: Hard Expo floors and downtown blocks add up — swap shoes nightly to help reduce blister risk by mid-week. Backup battery pack: Demo notes, session alerts, and badge QR codes can drain your phone before the Extra Innings Party. Water bottle: Colorado dryness can hit harder at 5,280 feet — refill between sessions, even when thirst is easy to ignore. Immune basics: Hand sanitizer and throat lozenges help when keynotes pack thousands into one hall. Warm layer: Afternoon sun feels mild; breakout rooms and Coors Field evenings don't. Lip balm and moisturizer: Dry Colorado air may leave skin and lips dry. Getting from the airport to the Content Marketing World venue Most attendees arrive via Denver International Airport (DEN), about 25 miles northeast of downtown Denver.[5][8] The Colorado Convention Center doesn't operate a complimentary airport shuttle — plan your transfer before you land. When your schedule allows, fly in on Sunday, Oct. 4. You may find it easier to collect your badge ahead of Monday Science & Magic Summit programming with less same-day arrival pressure — and give your body a night to adjust to altitude before a full conference day. Option Time Cost Notes RTD A Line (commuter rail) About 37 minutes to Union Station[8] About $10.50[9] Then 10–15 minutes walking or free MallRide bus to the convention center; check RTD Next Ride app for downtown rail construction alerts[11] Rideshare or taxi 30–40 minutes About $30–$50+, higher with traffic[5] Usually the fastest door-to-door option; pickup at designated DEN rideshare zones Shared shuttle (third party) 40–60 minutes About $25–$35 per person Several hotel drop-offs; budget extra time if you don't mind sharing the ride For a single traveler arriving on a weekday, the A Line often beats rideshare on cost for solo travelers — DEN is far enough that rail savings matter; I-70 traffic can erase a car's time advantage. Rideshare works for late arrivals, groups, or hotels outside the walkable downtown core. Beyond sessions: Make time for the Expo Hall and hallway conversations You'll find lots of vendor evaluations and opportunities for creator introductions on the Expo floor — in martech demos, summit hallway lines, and queue-side chats not on the official schedule. Expo Hall: Martech booths, light bites at the Monday reception, and casual conversations that often advance RFP timelines faster than email threads[2] Science & Magic Summit: WARC and Contagious programming on cultural trends — worth blocking Monday if you hold an All Access Pass[2] Marketing Effectiveness Summit: Effie-led sessions on insight and measurable creative — plan Tuesday around this if effectiveness is your team's gap[2] Extra Innings Party at Coors Field: Official Tuesday evening event — treat it as scheduled networking, not optional downtime[2] AI in Action Summit: Wednesday workshops and certification for teams building AI into content workflows[2] Download the CMI Events app early and star Expo Hall vendors you want to revisit — floor traffic peaks between keynotes when everyone heads the same direction at once. Network like you're building pipeline Treat Content Marketing World networking as a content-strategy project, not hallway luck. Before Denver: Build a list of 10 to 15 targets — peers comparing the same martech stack, creators you follow, analysts covering your category — and send a focused meeting note about two weeks out. During sessions and Expo walks: Start with the campaign problem you're solving, not a pitch deck. Write one actionable note per contact before you leave the conversation. Each evening: Draft brief follow-ups while details are fresh, then send within 48 hours with a specific ask — a shared brief, a 20-minute call, or an intro to your content ops lead. Hold a 30-minute follow-up block on Wednesday before your flight home. Responses slow down once you're buried in post-conference campaign reviews. Leave gaps in your schedule. A short reset at your hotel or a slow loop on the 16th Street Mall may work better than cramming breakouts wall-to-wall — and mile-high dryness makes hydration breaks worth prioritizing by day two. What to eat at Content Marketing World 2026 Three days walking the Expo Hall, summit hallways, and downtown blocks between sessions burn more energy than back-to-back Zoom marathons. Eat at the Expo receptions when your pass includes them, keep protein snacks in your bag, and drink water steadily — Colorado dryness hits harder at 5,280 feet than the convention hall air suggests. When you need table service, these downtown addresses fit different CMWorld moments: Client dinner: Guard and Grace on California Street offers private rooms a few blocks from the Colorado Convention Center.[13] Team meal: Rioja on Larimer Square offers Mediterranean-inspired sharing plates in a relaxed setting for group meals without white-tablecloth formality.[14] Executive lunch or one-on-one: Guard and Grace serves lunch Tuesday through Thursday for power-lunch conversations steps from downtown hotels.[13] Quick fuel between sessions: Hyatt Regency cafés and 16th Street Mall grab-and-go options keep you fed without leaving the downtown core when Expo hours are tight. Finish strong on departure day Leaving Denver cleanly matters as much as the sessions you attended. Handle these tasks before you head to DEN so re-entry at the office is smoother. Wrap up Denver before you head to DEN: Night-before prep: Charge gear, set out Wednesday travel clothes, and sweep the room for badges, chargers, and Expo handouts. Late checkout: Ask at check-in if your flight leaves after 3 p.m. and confirm again Tuesday night. You can also have Navan Edge request on your behalf. DEN timing: Post-conference Monday mornings stack up at security — plan two hours domestic, three international. Expense upload: File receipts within 48 hours of checkout and flag any nightly rate above your lodging cap. Lounge window: Use card lounge access to organize session notes before boarding. Team debrief: Block 60 minutes Thursday to translate Content Marketing World notes into Q4 content priorities. Make your Content Marketing World 2026 trip count Content Marketing World 2026 rewards advance planning for things like onPeak housing, a timed open booking, a Denver budget checked against FY2027 per diem, attending Expo Hall and summit blocks beside must-see sessions, and starting follow-up before you leave the area. title: Using LIMS to Deliver a Better Customer Experience with Client Portals
summary: Learn how LIMS client portals improve transparency, automate COA delivery, and enhance customer experience for compliant, modern laboratories. Learn more on Confident LIMS
body_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE – November 12 2025 San Francisco, CA — A LIMS with an integrated client portal transforms laboratory customer experience by providing real-time access to sample status, Certificates of Analysis (COAs), and reports—enhancing transparency, turnaround time, and client satisfaction. 🎧 Prefer to listen? Here’s the audio version of this article: Your browser does not support the audio element. Introduction: Put Your Clients at the Center of Your Lab Laboratory operations don’t end when a test result is generated. Today’s lab customers expect the same transparency and convenience they’re accustomed to in other digital services. When results are slow or communication is opaque, clients can lose trust—and look elsewhere for their testing needs. Investing in a modern Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) with a client portal turns customer experience from an afterthought into a competitive advantage. By providing real-time access to sample status and results, labs differentiate themselves on service, not just science. Faster turnaround times and clear communication lead to greater loyalty and repeat business. ‍ Why Client Portals Drive Growth 1. Time Is Money: Faster COA Delivery Traditional methods of emailing test results or manually uploading PDFs delay delivery of critical data. A LIMS client portal automatically generates the Certificate of Analysis (COA) and provides immediate access once results are approved, helping clients act quickly and confidently. 2. Transparency Builds Trust Real-time status updates show where each sample is in the testing process—received, in progress, or complete—reducing “where are my results?” inquiries and reinforcing your lab’s reliability and professionalism. 3. Consistency and Professionalism A portal standardizes report formats and ensures secure delivery every time. Clients know exactly where to look and how to retrieve their data, which enhances satisfaction and streamlines operations. ‍ How Does a Confident LIMS Client Portal Work? - COA Delivery Once testing is complete and quality checks are approved, the system automatically generates a COA with your lab’s branding. Clients log into the portal and download the report instantly—no emails, attachments, or extra steps required. - PDF Auto-Generation for Compliance Regulatory frameworks like ISO 17025 , FSMA , and 21 CFR Part 11 often require precise PDF formats for recordkeeping. Confident LIMS automatically converts approved results into compliant PDFs, saving staff time and ensuring documentation consistency. - Real-Time Test Status Updates When clients submit samples, they can see clear progress indicators such as received , preparing , analyzing , and ready for review . This visibility reduces anxiety, eliminates status calls, and allows your team to focus on testing rather than follow-ups. ‍ Beyond Convenience: What Clients Really Want Clients choose labs that not only deliver accurate results but also make their work easier. A seamless portal experience reduces friction and shows that your lab is invested in their success. It also: Shortens sales cycles by demonstrating professionalism early in the customer journey. Encourages repeat orders through a consistent, transparent experience. Boosts referrals as satisfied clients share positive experiences. In regulated industries like pharma , cannabis , and food testing , a compliant and transparent customer interface is now expected—not optional. ‍ Compliance and Data Integrity Benefits A LIMS client portal also strengthens compliance posture by: Maintaining a complete audit trail of report generation and client access. Ensuring immutable PDF records that align with ISO 17025 and 21 CFR Part 11. Providing role-based access controls for secure client logins. By automating these processes, labs stay audit-ready and protect both client data and accreditation status. ‍ Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) - What is a LIMS client portal? A LIMS client portal is a secure online platform where lab customers can track sample progress, access Certificates of Analysis, and download results in real time. - How does a client portal improve customer experience? It gives clients instant visibility into testing workflows, eliminates manual result sharing, and fosters transparency—reducing emails and turnaround delays. - Is a LIMS client portal compliant with industry regulations? Yes. Confident LIMS automatically generates compliant, non-editable PDFs and maintains full audit trails that meet ISO 17025 , FSMA , and 21 CFR Part 11 requirements. - Can smaller labs implement client portals easily? Absolutely. Confident LIMS is designed for ease of use and quick deployment—bringing enterprise-level transparency to labs of any size. ‍ Conclusion: Elevate Service, Elevate Growth Great science isn’t enough to keep clients coming back. In a market where accuracy and timelines are equally matched, superior service becomes your differentiator. A LIMS with an integrated client portal positions your lab as a true partner—deepening trust, streamlining workflows, and driving sustainable growth through better customer experience. ‍ See a Client Portal in Action Want to see how a client portal can transform your lab’s customer experience? 👉 Book a Demo to explore how Confident’s client portal enhances transparency, shortens turnaround time, and helps your lab grow with confidence. 🎧 Listen on Spotify: Hear this topic discussed in our latest podcast episode below.

title: Priority Commerce Launches SeatGeek Integration to Help Sports Organizations Power Connected Commerce with One View - Total Command
summary: ALPHARETTA, Ga. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- Priority Commerce today announced a production-ready integration with global ticketing leader SeatGeek that gives sports and entertainment organizations access to Priority Commerce’s advanced payment capabilities.
body_text: Priority Commerce Launches SeatGeek Integration to Help Teams and Venues Reduce Payment Costs August 4, 2026 PDF Version ALPHARETTA, Ga.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- Priority Commerce today announced a production-ready integration with global ticketing leader SeatGeek that gives sports and entertainment organizations access to Priority Commerce’s advanced payment capabilities. The integration gives SeatGeek’s roster of more than 100 partners—including teams, venues, leagues, and other enterprise ticketing clients—the option to use Priority Commerce for payment processing. At the core of the integration is Priority Commerce’s support for Level III transaction data, an advanced business-to-business standard that captures detailed line-item information. This capability allows participating SeatGeek partners to significantly reduce payment processing costs by unlocking lower interchange rates on eligible commercial card transactions. In addition to cost savings, the integration connects Priority Commerce’s payment infrastructure directly with SeatGeek’s platform to support both card-not-present and card-present transactions. The result is a seamless payment experience across the full ticketing commerce ecosystem. “Modern sports and entertainment organizations need a commerce partner that provides total command of their payments environment,” said Tom Priore, CEO of Priority Commerce. “This integration delivers the advanced tools teams and venues need to maximize their cash flow and optimize operational control to drive higher profits.” “Priority Commerce is a strong addition to the SeatGeek platform,” said Chris Sanger, VP of Payments & Compliance at SeatGeek. “It gives our partners more choice in how they manage their payment operations, and access to new financial tools.” About Priority Commerce Priority Commerce delivers payments and banking solutions that power connected commerce. Through a unified platform of payables, merchant services, and banking and treasury, we help businesses manage money more effectively and unlock growth. The Priority Commerce Engine accelerates cash flow, improves working capital, reduces costs, and creates new revenue opportunities. Learn more about Priority Commerce (NASDAQ: PRTH) at prioritycommerce.com . About SeatGeek SeatGeek was founded in 2009 when three live event fans had the crazy idea that modern technology could improve the live event-going experience for everyone – fans, teams, and artists. Today, SeatGeek offers a trusted marketplace for fans to easily buy and sell tickets to the events they love and provides primary box office technology for some of the most prominent names in sports and entertainment globally.
