title: How Cloud Connected AI Products Run On-Prem
summary: The Purdue Model explained: every level from PLC to DMZ, the companies that run on it, and how AI deploys into segmented OT networks.
body_text: Daniel Reiff Published Aug 7, 2026 • 7 min read Summary The Purdue Model splits an industrial network into levels (physical process, PLCs, SCADA, MES, the DMZ, then enterprise IT) so a breach in business software never reaches the machinery, and it still underpins ISA-95, IEC 62443, and most heavy-industry networks today. A cloud-native AI platform can deploy into it without breaking segmentation: Roboflow runs inference at the edge, fully air-gapped, through a brokered DMZ gateway, or over the API, matching whichever posture the network enforces. In manufacturing , if you are operating an IT/OT network, you’ve probably heard of the Purdue Model . Providing a reference model for how sensors, controllers, and systems all connect, it ensures the plant runs smoothly. In doing so, it institutes a separation between IT and OT, isolating controls. This separation causes every enterprise OT buyer to eventually ask the same question: How does a cloud-native AI platform deploy into a network built to never phone home? It's a fair question. The plant floor wasn't built to trust the internet, and for good reason. Working alongside Fortune 500 partners, Roboflow has developed a flexible deployment model for AI products. We deploy systems across levels of OT, in the DMZ, and air gapped to meet the requirements of today’s industrial network architecture. Before we dive in depth on how it works, let’s start with the model most industrial networks are still built on. What Is the Purdue Model? The Purdue Model (formally the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture) is the mental map industrial security has run on for thirty years. Its job is simple to state and hard to do: keep the systems that run physical machinery separated from the systems that run the business, so a bad day in IT never becomes a dangerous day in OT. It does this by slicing the network into layers, each with its own level of operational and informational control. The key idea is "adjacency": a level only talks to the layer directly above and below it. If an attacker lands on the corporate email server up top, strict separation means they're several controlled hops away from the controller that opens a valve. Segmentation contains the blast radius. What lives at each level: Level 0, the physical process. The machinery itself: sensors, actuators, motors, valves, the equipment doing the real work. This is where bits meet the physical world. Level 1, basic control. The PLCs and RTUs that read Level 0 sensors and send back commands. This is the reflex layer, translating a signal into an action thousands of times a second. Level 2, supervisory control. SCADA , DCS, and the HMIs where an operator watches and steers the process. If Level 1 is reflexes, Level 2 is the cockpit. Level 3, manufacturing operations. MES and historians, the systems that coordinate production rather than individual machines and store the record of what happened. This is the top of the OT world. Level 3.5, the DMZ. The demilitarized zone: firewalls, proxies, jump servers, and data brokers that sit between OT and IT. Nothing crosses from the plant to the enterprise, or back, without passing through here and being inspected. This is the border checkpoint. Level 4, enterprise network. Business applications, logistics, email, the site's IT infrastructure. Corporate, but plant-adjacent. Level 5, corporate IT. ERP , directory services, data centers, the internet. The outside world. The dividing line that matters most runs between Level 3 and Level 4: the IT/OT boundary, enforced through the DMZ. Above it is business software, where a breach costs money and downtime. Below it is a physical process, where a breach can cost a limb or a life. That asymmetry is why the model exists. Who Runs on This Model? Almost everyone in heavy industry, but very few say so on the record, and that's by design. Publishing your exact level structure is handing an attacker a map to your DMZ. So the honest answer comes in two shapes. The institutional answer: if a company follows ISA-95, IEC 62443, NIST SP 800-82, or the Cisco/Rockwell Converged Plantwide Ethernet (CPwE) architecture, it's running a Purdue-derived network whether it uses the word or not. ISA-95 says outright that it "relies on the well-known Purdue Reference Model." The named answer: a smaller set has put Purdue in writing. ExxonMobil has publicly described challenging the model's historical assumptions, which is itself proof their installed base is Purdue-structured. Georgia-Pacific's own patents reference the "Purdue Model for ICS security" as a required protocol. Phillips 66 and Honeywell wrote Purdue levels directly into granted patent claims. Even the modern players lean on it: Anduril hires OT network engineers to "design segmented architectures based on ISA-95 and Purdue Model principles," and Microsoft's guidance for extending OT to Azure is built around Purdue's six levels. It shows up everywhere from oil refineries to hyperscale data-center mechanical systems. Is It Outdated, Or Still Relevant? The original model, drawn up in 1990, assumed OT would stay air-gapped forever, physically walled off from IT and the internet. That assumption has collapsed. Plants now want their operational data in the cloud for analytics and their AI on the floor for efficiency. IT and OT are converging whether the security architecture likes it or not. The Colonial Pipeline attack made the stakes concrete: the intrusion was in IT, but the impact landed on operations. So is Purdue obsolete? No, but the way you enforce it has to evolve. The consensus keeps the layers and stops trusting position alone. The reimagined model puts modern controls on top of the old hierarchy: Zero-trust segmentation : instead of assuming a device is safe because of where it sits, verify what it's doing. Allow only the transactions that are needed, and monitor everything. Visibility first: you can't secure what you can't see. As plants add IoT and edge devices, knowing each device's normal behavior is what lets you catch the abnormal one. Deliberate convergence: cross-layer communication is now necessary, but it should be brokered and logged, never a flat network that happens to work. The layers still describe where things are. Zero trust describes whether they're allowed to talk. You need both now. How Does It Coexist with AI? AI is where there is tension, because AI breaks the adjacency rule by nature. An edge inference model has to act down at Level 1 or 2, right next to the machinery, but it also needs to learn, which means sending data upstream to retrain and improve. A copilot reads from the cloud data lake and writes suggestions back to the SCADA console. A vision model runs inference at the edge and ships flagged images out for review. That's cross-layer data movement in real time, as a core function of the product, exactly what Purdue was built to prevent. Deploy it carelessly and you've drilled a hole straight through your segmentation. Deploy it thoughtfully and you get the efficiency without giving up the boundary. The difference is in how the AI system moves data and models across the layers, which makes it a product-architecture question more than a security-policy one. What a Purdue-Friendly AI System Requires If you take the model seriously, it becomes a checklist. Any AI or computer vision system that wants to live in a segmented industrial network has to be capable of these things, not all at once, but able to, so each site can pick the shape that fits its posture: Run where the work is: inference has to execute inside the OT zone, at the edge , next to the process, not only in a distant cloud. Latency and segmentation both demand it. Keep runtime data in-zone by default: live process data (camera feeds, PLC signals, inference results) should never have to cross the IT/OT boundary just to keep the system running. A plant that allows no outbound internet at all should still get a fully functional system. Move models across the boundary with flexibility: new models and workflows have to be able to enter the OT zone in whatever form the network trusts, as reviewable, injectable packages where a live API dependency isn't welcome, or over the API where it is. Either way, the crossing adapts to the network's rules instead of asking the network to adapt to it. Be observable: operators and security teams need visibility into every edge device (what it's running, whether it's healthy, what it's doing) to support a zero-trust posture. How Roboflow Delivers Secure AI for Enterprises We're an end-to-end computer vision platform for building the applications that run on a plant floor: defect detection, visual inspection, assembly verification , process monitoring, and measurement. These are the problems process-analytics AI can't touch, because they require seeing. A vision model is fast becoming a standard tool in the process engineer's kit. We fit a Purdue network because we don't insist on one deployment shape. We offer a range of postures that map onto where a customer sits, and onto the requirements above: IT and cloud batch: for workloads that live above the boundary, push image batches to our managed cloud and pull predictions back. No on-prem computer required. OT with API: pull models and workflows down through the API, run inference on-prem, and send images back out when the network permits. Inference happens where the work is, and egress is allowed but not required. OT air-gapped: for sites that strictly enforce the boundary, inference runs with no internet at all. Models and workflows are injected as artifacts, over a GitOps pipeline or physical media, and runtime data (camera to inference to PLC) never crosses the gap. DMZ and secure gateway: pull models and return data through one brokered proxy in the DMZ, a single logged egress point instead of scattered connections. The same gateway gives security teams remote visibility into edge devices. The through-line is deployment flexibility as a security feature. A customer that won't allow a single outbound packet gets air-gapped inference. A customer that wants centralized model management with controlled data flow gets the secure gateway. A customer comfortable with the cloud gets the API. Same platform, same models, different posture, chosen to match their segmentation instead of fighting it. The Purdue Model isn't an obstacle to deploying AI. It's a specification, and we built Roboflow to meet it. title: How to keep your procurement skills sharp in the AI era
summary: AI skill atrophy is real. A former procurement leader on over-reliance, misplaced trust, and which skills to keep sharp, with new data from 1,050 leaders.
body_text: My phone died on vacation this summer in Venice, a city I did not know well, with three generations of my family waiting on me for directions. “I know,” I said. "We can use a map!" I quickly discovered that I am actually not as good at reading and navigating with maps as I used to be. This is an effect known as ‘ skill atrophy ,’ and I couldn’t shake the feeling that the same thing is happening right now with AI at work. Three generations and one dead phone battery Up until the phone unceremoniously ran out of battery we had navigated that entire trip by GPS, the way most people do in their day-to-day. As you know, all you have to do is type an address into your phone and your Maps app finds the fastest path, be it walking or driving. But as our phone battery went, so did the maps. To use a paper map was a genuinely novel concept for my son, who has never needed to in his life. For him, this was a new challenge. For my mom, who did not grow up with cell phones, it seemed perfectly normal. What I found interesting was how this clash of generational skills affected me. I grew up navigating long road trips with a giant book of maps. but at this point this is merely embedded in muscle memory. Could I still do it? Yes! Was it as easy as I remembered? It was not. My ability to navigate with a map instead of GPS had clearly weakened, as if the skill had atrophied over time. The same thing happened when we tried to calculate a tip at a restaurant. I also did not grow up with a calculator in my pocket, so doing math in one’s head was simply expected. Same with phone numbers and birthdays; before cell phones, I memorized my friends' numbers so I could reach them from anywhere. Once my phone remembered them for me, my ability to do so diminished year after year. Why AI skill atrophy matters at work AI has become a necessary tool for productivity. In Zip's State of AI in Spend 2026 survey of 1,050 procurement, finance, IT, and operations leaders, 62% said they use AI tools multiple times per day. AI is well past the experiment phase; it is quite literally how work gets done today. And in some cases, these tools can cause you to lose skills you previously had. Take the common use case of writing an executive summary of a project. Before AI, this was a manual task that required real thought. You had to know the high-level story of the project, understand the audience so you could tailor the message, and condense everything into a format that got to the key issues. Now an executive summary is a click away. That is a huge time saver to be sure, and the productivity gains are real; 89% of leaders in the same survey report a net-positive productivity effect from AI, even after accounting for the time spent reviewing and correcting its output. Sounds like a solid win. But can it lead to skill atrophy? Possibly. If I no longer regularly work through those questions myself, I may lose some of that ability over time. Most professionals are not worried about this yet. Half of surveyed leaders say AI is augmenting their skills while their skill set stays largely the same, and 32% say AI is helping them develop new skills faster. But 12% report a mixed effect: AI helps in some areas while they lose sharpness in others. That 12% is describing exactly what I felt holding that paper map. So what we have to ask ourselves now is does it matter? The risk of over-reliance on AI tools I would argue it matters. Going back to my examples, technology often fails. What if I lose access to my AI tools at the moment I need to produce a summary? Am I so reliant on AI that I can no longer do the task at all, even less efficiently? This is not a hypothetical. When leaders were asked what would happen if their primary AI tool were unavailable for a single workday, 72% said they would feel at least a moderate hit to their productivity, and 29% said the impact would be significant or severe. One workday. And sometimes you do not have the tool in the moment that the question arises. Have you ever been cornered in a meeting and asked to summarize a project you had not prepared for? Can you respond effectively without saying you need to go back to your desk and ask AI for help? Why fact-checking AI output is the skill to build There is a second side to this, which is that many people who have not embraced AI at work hold back because they do not trust what the tool produces. That skepticism keeps them from real productivity gains. What often gets overlooked is the opposite side of the coin. What happens when you lose the underlying skills and rely on AI outputs with no ability to question the result? A good example is the navigation app Waze. It gives you the optimal route based on live traffic. Have you ever blindly followed Waze only to find its "optimal" route asking you to make an unprotected left across multiple lanes of rush-hour traffic? Follow those directions without question and you may sit at that intersection for a very long time. The same applies to AI. If you follow its output blindly because you have lost the ability to interrogate it, you may end up on a longer or incorrect path. Leaders seem to sense this. When asked which capability their teams most need to develop for an AI-driven environment, the top answer, at 49%, was evaluating and fact-checking AI-generated analysis. The skill of the next few years is the discernment and base-level expertise to know whether the answer AI gives is actually correct. Why AI over-reliance is a business continuity risk I spent the majority of my career as a procurement practitioner and leader. I know business is rarely this simple. Reliance on technology is normal; over-reliance can be catastrophic. In the earlier days of the software industry, procurement and security professionals focused heavily on disaster recovery. What happens to the business if this piece of technology stops working? How do we stay afloat? AI may not require a disaster recovery plan in the traditional sense, but the same discipline applies. And most organizations are not there: only 31% of leaders say they are very confident in their business continuity if a critical AI system failed. Over-reliance and skill erosion are a continuity risk of their own, just one that shows up in people instead of servers. None of this argues for using AI less; it still has tremendous upside. Be deliberate about which skills you keep sharp, so that when the battery dies, you can still read the map. The data in this article comes from Zip's State of AI in Spend 2026, a survey of 1,050 procurement, finance, IT, and operations leaders fielded April to May 2026. Download the full report.

title: Firm AI Principle 7: The firm’s memory and methods are the moat.
summary: Intapp introduces Firm AI — the AI category built for the business of a professional services firm, not just the individual professionals inside it. Accessing and fully leveraging the firm’s memory and methods is what truly differentiates.
body_text: In our final installment of the Firm AI Principles series, we discuss what truly differentiates a firm and gives it competitive advantage: its collective experience over time, and unique approach to serving clients and running the business of the firm. Principle 7: The firm’s memory and methods are the moat. Two things compound inside a great firm: its memory of every matter, deal, engagement, relationship, and decision it has ever made, and the unwritten methods by which it turns all of that into the next decision. Horizontal AI sees neither. Firm AI is how the firm finally captures both. The firm’s most unique experience is encoded in the record of every decision it has ever made — every deal walked away from, every lateral hired or passed over, every fee arrangement held or broken, every conflict cleared or escalated, every relationship deepened or allowed to lapse — and the years of partner and MD correspondence that captures the reasoning behind each one. From a firm growth standpoint, this is the strategic asset that encodes what the firm actually knows. The firm’s memory is also not a single pool. It is a governed Venn diagram of segments — matter teams, deal teams, fund vehicles, audit engagements — each with its own access list, walls, and retention posture. A useful Firm AI reads across segments where permitted, redacts where it must, and elevates cross-firm patterns (methodology, expertise, opportunity benchmarks) without violating any segment’s promise to its client, LP, or regulator. Segment-aware memory is what lets the firm draw on its own history without betraying the rules under which the history was built. What distinguishes one firm from another is the method. The method is the franchise. But memory is more than artifacts. It is method. Every firm has a way of making decisions that lives nowhere written down: the senior partner’s instinct for which deals are worth the reputational risk, the managing partner’s unwritten rules about which clients earn reduced-rate work, the fund CIO’s pattern for when to walk away from a promising target. Legal advice and deal-making are commodities. What distinguishes one firm from another is the method. The method is the franchise. For a century, the method has been passed down in apprenticeship — corridor conversations, the editing of a first-draft memo in red pen, the way a senior partner reframes a push-back. There was no way to codify it. Firm playbooks are the first vehicle that can. Authored by the firm, run by expert coworker agents, governed by the firm’s compliance posture, improved every time used. Codified, the method is not a replacement for culture; it is the way the firm scales its culture without diluting it. A firm that does this keeps its method when its senior partners retire. A firm that does not watches the method walk out the door. And the method improves itself by being used. Take a private capital firm that, for the first time, screens all of its inbound deals against its own thesis. Every deal it reviews, and every call it makes to pursue or pass, becomes part of the record. The firm builds a proprietary history of its own judgment — what it chased, what it declined, and why — that no competitor has and no model can supply. The next screen is sharper than the last, not because the model improved, but because the firm’s own decisions trained it. This is the flywheel, and it is why the moat deepens over time. The firm gets smarter about itself the longer it operates. When the next generation of foundation models arrives, the firm that has compounded years of its own judgment is years ahead. Horizontal AI cannot compound inside the firm the same way, because it cannot see what makes the firm a firm. Firm AI compounds. The moat gets deeper every quarter. title: Synthesia · Cinder case study
summary: How Synthesia extended its trust & safety stack with Cinder — moderating every AI video script before a frame is rendered, scaling automated review to 11.5M+ items in 2025, and keeping enforcement at the speed of its roadmap.
body_text: Synthesia’s trust and safety team has been doing this work for years and knows its policies, edge cases, and customer base better than anyone. What it needs now is infrastructure that can keep pace with how quickly the product and the threat landscape are moving, which is why Synthesia is combining its know-how with Cinder's technological capabilities. Cinder gives Synthesia an in-house agent that acts as a second pass on every model decision, gathering context, reconciling signals, and only escalating to a human reviewer when there is genuinely a judgement call to make. Cinder’s classifiers evaluate every script in line, before a frame is rendered. Every action a reviewer takes becomes a signal that retrains the system, so the model sharpens week after week. Equally important, Cinder is built for product velocity. When Synthesia launches new avatar types, new languages, or new product surfaces, the trust and safety team can move at the pace of the roadmap. Each year, Synthesia publishes Futuresafe , its annual responsible creation report, so customers, regulators, and the public can see how the system performs in detail. The 2025 edition documents the scale at which Synthesia existing systems already operate, and gives a clear picture of the foundation Cinder is now extending. In 2025, Synthesia’s automated moderation tooling reviewed more than 11.5 million pieces of content and removed 841,957 of them where they violated Synthesia’s Acceptable Use Policy or Content Moderation Policies. Manual review handled a further 382,792 items and removed 70,272. Across all customer segments, 787 accounts were terminated for repeated violations. Automated moderation volume grew by roughly 77% between 2024 and 2025, from 6.56 million items to 11.58 million, reflecting both platform growth and a deliberate shift towards catching issues earlier in the workflow. Automated removals more than doubled in the same period, from 314,403 to 841,957. At the same time, the volume of content reaching human review fell from 792,586 to 441,086, and manual removals fell from 138,692 to 70,272. This is the pattern Synthesia has been working towards for years. AI handles the obvious cases at scale, while human reviewers concentrate on appeals, ambiguous cases, and the high-stakes decisions where their judgement matters most. Trust in Synthesia’s appeals process shows up in the numbers as well. Synthesia processed 12,450 user appeals in 2025. Around 31% were approved on review and the original decision was reversed, while around 69% were upheld. This is the distribution expected from a system that catches genuine violations consistently while still leaving room for legitimate use cases to be reinstated when a classifier gets a call wrong.

title: What Are the Dimensions of Popular Storage Unit Sizes in Orlando?
summary: Popular storage unit sizes in Orlando include 5×5, 5×10, 5×15, 10×10, 10×15, 10×20, 10×25, and 10×30. These sizes range from about 25 square feet of floor space for a 5×5 unit to about 300 square feet for a 10×30 unit. body_text: Popular storage unit sizes in Orlando include 5×5, 5×10, 5×15, 10×10, 10×15, 10×20, 10×25, and 10×30 . These sizes range from about 25 square feet of floor space for a 5×5 unit to about 300 square feet for a 10×30 unit. For folks living in Orlando, picking the right storage unit size usually depends on your location and why you need more room. If you’re in an apartment in areas like Downtown Orlando, College Park, or Baldwin Park , a 5×5 or 5×10 unit might be all you need for some extra space. However, if you’re moving, renovating, or downsizing, you might want to consider a larger unit like a 10×15, 10×20, or even bigger . Popular Storage Unit Sizes in Orlando Unit Size Floor Space Comparable Size Common Uses 5×5 25 sq. ft. Large closet Boxes, seasonal items, small furniture 5×10 75 sq. ft. Walk-in closet Small bedroom or apartment belongings 5×15 112 sq. ft. Large walk-in closet Furniture, appliances, and boxes 10×10 100 sq. ft. Large shed Contents of multiple rooms 10×15 150 sq. ft. Large bedroom Furniture and belongings from several rooms 10×20 200 sq. ft. Small one-car garage Contents of a three-bedroom home 10×25 250 sq. ft. Larger than a one-car garage Contents of a three- to four-bedroom home 10×30 300 sq. ft. Large household storage space Contents of a four- to five-bedroom home Storage unit dimensions are generally expressed as width by length . Exact dimensions and ceiling heights can vary by Orlando facility and individual unit. What Are the Dimensions of a 5×5 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 5×5 storage unit offers a cozy 25 square feet of space, similar in size to a large closet. It’s the perfect solution for Orlando apartment dwellers needing a bit of extra space for: Storage bins Holiday decor Seasonal clothing Small furniture Sporting equipment Personal items If you’re living in an apartment or condo in neighborhoods such as Downtown Orlando, Thornton Park, College Park, or South Eola , this size provides just the right amount of storage without the need to rent much more space than necessary. What Are the Dimensions of a 5×10 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 5×10 storage unit spans around 75 square feet of floor space , offering a versatile area for your belongings. This layout is perfect for fitting larger items and bulkier possessions like: Sofas and chairs Mattresses and bed frames Appliances Dressers Boxes and household items This size can be an excellent choice for Orlando residents who have outgrown smaller units but don’t quite need the larger 100-square-foot space of a 10×10 unit. What Are the Dimensions of a 5×15 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 5×15 storage unit offers about 112 square feet of floor space , making it a versatile choice for storing various items. This size, larger than a typical storage closet, can easily accommodate: Sofas and living room furniture Bedroom sets Mattresses Dining furniture Household appliances Boxes and storage containers For Orlando residents transitioning between apartments or homes, renovating, or needing temporary storage for several rooms’ worth of belongings, a 5×15 unit provides ample space without the need for one of the largest unit sizes. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×15 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 10×15 storage unit measures approximately 10 feet wide by 15 feet long , providing about 150 square feet of floor space . This size may accommodate furniture and belongings from several rooms, including: Living room furniture Bedroom sets Major appliances Dining furniture Mattresses Boxes A 10×15 unit can be useful during a move or home renovation when a 10×10 does not provide enough space. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×20 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 10×20 storage unit gives you about 200 square feet of space, similar to the size of a one-car garage —pretty spacious, right? It’s perfect for storing the contents of a three-bedroom Orlando home, accommodating your furniture, appliances, mattresses, and plenty of boxes. Whether you’re tackling a big move, undergoing renovations, or in-between homes, this unit size offers the roominess you need to keep everything safe and sound. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×25 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 10×25 storage unit gives you around 250 square feet of space, measuring about 10 feet wide by 25 feet long . It’s ideal for holding everything from a three- to four-bedroom home , depending on how much stuff you have and how big it is. This unit has plenty of room for large furniture, appliances, bedroom setups, dining furniture, lots of boxes, and various household items. For Orlando families making a big move or storing most of their home’s contents during renovations, having those extra five feet compared to a 10×20 can make all the difference in comfortably fitting your belongings. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×30 Storage Unit in Orlando? A 10×30 storage unit offers roughly 300 square feet of space, measuring about 10 feet wide by 30 feet long . As one of the largest storage options around, it’s perfect for holding items from a four- to five-bedroom home —depending on how much you have and their sizes. This size is especially handy for big moves in Orlando, extensive renovations, or when you need to store furniture, appliances, boxes, and a whole lot more all together. What Should Orlando Residents Consider When Choosing a Storage Unit Size? When picking a storage unit in Orlando, there are a few things to think about aside from size. You’ll want to consider what you’re storing, how long you’ll keep it there, and how frequently you’ll need to access your items . Start by measuring your larger items like sofas, mattresses, dining tables, and appliances, then figure out how many boxes or storage bins you’ll need for everything else. And don’t forget about Orlando’s heat, humidity, and those rainy days ! If your belongings are sensitive to moisture or temperature swings, a climate-controlled unit might be your best bet to keep everything safe. Lastly, think about location—you’ll probably want your storage unit conveniently close to your home, apartment, workplace, or on your regular route. This way, popping in and out for your items will be a breeze! What Size Storage Unit Do I Need in Orlando? As a general guide: 5×5: Good for boxes, seasonal belongings, and small furniture 5×10: Useful for a bedroom’s contents or additional apartment storage 5×15: Provides more room for furniture, appliances, and boxes 10×10: Can accommodate furniture and belongings from multiple rooms 10×15: Useful for larger moves and multi-room storage 10×20: About the footprint of a one-car garage and may hold the contents of a three-bedroom home 10×25: May accommodate belongings from a three- to four-bedroom home 10×30: Provides ample space for belongings from a four- to five-bedroom home These are general estimates. The amount of space you need will depend on the size, number, and arrangement of your belongings. Frequently Asked Questions About Storage Unit Sizes in Orlando What is the most common storage unit size in Orlando? Orlando storage facilities offer a range of sizes, with options commonly including 5×5, 5×10, 10×10, 10×15, 10×20 , and other configurations. Availability varies by facility. How big is a 10×10 storage unit in Orlando? A 10×10 storage unit provides approximately 100 square feet of floor space . Its footprint is roughly half the size of a one-car garage and can provide space for furniture, appliances, boxes, and belongings from multiple rooms. What size storage unit do I need for an Orlando apartment? For a small amount of apartment overflow, a 5×5 may be sufficient. A 5×10 or 5×15 provides additional room for furniture and boxes, while a 10×10 may be more appropriate when storing the contents of multiple rooms. The right size depends on the amount and dimensions of your belongings. What size storage unit do I need for a one-bedroom Orlando home? A 5×10 or 5×15 storage unit is well-suited to fit the contents of a one-bedroom Orlando home or apartment. This includes bedroom furniture like beds, dressers, and nightstands, as well as small appliances such as microwaves, air conditioners, or televisions. There’s also room for boxes filled with personal items, clothing, kitchenware, and books, along with other household belongings like lamps, small tables, and rugs. Choosing between these sizes will depend on how much stuff you have and the dimensions of each item you’re planning to store. What size storage unit do I need for a two-bedroom Orlando home? A 10×10 or 10×15 storage unit may accommodate the contents of a two-bedroom Orlando home or apartment, including bedroom and living room furniture, appliances, mattresses, and boxes. A 10×15 unit may be a better option if you have larger furniture or need additional storage space. What size storage unit do I need for a three-bedroom Orlando home? A 10×20 storage unit may accommodate the contents of a three-bedroom home, depending on the amount and size of the furniture, appliances, boxes, and other belongings being stored. Should I consider climate-controlled storage in Orlando? In Orlando, climate-controlled storage is often a crucial choice for protecting your belongings from the city’s intense heat, high humidity, and frequent moisture . Items like electronics, wooden furniture, artwork, photographs, important documents, and musical instruments can suffer damage from fluctuating temperatures and damp conditions. When deciding on storage features, think carefully about the nature of what you’re storing and how long it will be there. Opting for a climate-controlled unit can help ensure that your valuables remain in pristine condition, offering peace of mind regardless of Orlando’s weather swings.

title: Amazon SES now helps identify automated open and click events in event notifications
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Amazon SES now helps identify automated open and click events in event notifications
body_text: Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) now helps you identify automated email interactions. Open and Click event notifications now include an isBotEvent field that indicates whether the event was likely triggered by an automated system or a human recipient. Customers who publish Open or Click events through a configuration set event destination will now see an isBotEvent field with a value of Likely or Unlikely in event notifications. You can use this field as a signal to help you better understand how much of your engagement is driven by human recipients versus automated systems. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SES is available. If you already publish Open or Click events to an event destination, the isBotEvent field is automatically included, no additional configuration is needed. To learn more, see Contents of event data that Amazon SES publishes to Amazon SNS and Contents of event data that Amazon SES publishes to Firehose in the Amazon SES Developer Guide.

title: Top 10 Easy Ways to Make Money Online in India 2026

body_text: "Easy ways to make money online" is one of the most searched money phrases in India — and one of the most misused. Easy does not mean effortless, and it definitely does not mean instant. What it really means is a low barrier to entry : no capital, no office, no degree, and nothing more than the phone already in your hand. The difference between people who make ₹500 online and people who make ₹50,000 is rarely talent — it is choosing a method whose ceiling is worth their time, and sticking with it past the first slow month. This guide ranks the 10 genuinely easy ways to make money online in India in 2026. For each one you get what it really involves, realistic monthly earnings, and who it suits — so you can make the right call instead of hopping between apps. Earn by Selling Financial Products with GroMo (+ Refer & Earn) Estimated earning: ₹5,000–₹50,000+ per month. Ease: high — your phone and your contacts are the whole setup. Best overall on this list. GroMo turns something you already do — recommending things to friends and family — into a real income. You help people in your network get financial products they anyway need: savings accounts, credit cards, demat accounts, loans, and insurance from India's leading banks and regulated companies . When an application you referred is approved, the institution pays you a commission. A single approved credit card can pay ₹1,000–₹2,000+, which is more than most apps on this list pay in a month. The refer-and-earn layer makes it even easier to start: share a product link on WhatsApp, the customer completes the application digitally, and you track the approval and payout in the app. There is zero investment — no stock, no fees, no targets — and free training that teaches you how each product works before you recommend it. Why it is the best method here: it combines the easiest possible start (sharing links with people you know) with the highest earning ceiling, and it compounds — every satisfied customer becomes a source of repeat sales and referrals. You also build genuine financial knowledge that most people never get. 2. Freelancing on Fiverr, Upwork, and Internshala Estimated earning: ₹5,000–₹50,000+ per month. Ease: medium — needs one sellable skill. If you can write, design, edit video, code, translate, or manage spreadsheets, freelancing marketplaces connect you with clients worldwide. Start with small, clearly-scoped gigs, price low to win your first five reviews, then raise rates — most consistent freelancers roughly double their rate within six months. Payments are protected by the platform, so you are not chasing invoices. Right for you if: you already have a skill, or are willing to spend two weeks learning one properly on free resources before selling it. 3. Online Tutoring Estimated earning: ₹5,000–₹25,000 per month at ₹200–₹800 per hour. Ease: medium. Strong at maths, English, science, coding, or a competitive exam you have cleared? Vedantu, Chegg, Superprof, and even self-run WhatsApp batches pay well for structured teaching. Tutoring pays more per hour than almost anything else that needs no capital — and demand from parents is constant. Right for you if: you can explain things patiently and want an income that also sharpens your own knowledge. 4. Cashback and Easy Money-Making Apps Estimated earning: ₹500–₹3,000 per month. Ease: very high — the easiest real money online. Cashback and rewards apps pay small amounts for shopping you would do anyway, scanning receipts, or completing simple missions. The genuine ones pay small and pay on time. Treat this as a top-up, not an income: it is the easiest way to get money online, but the ceiling is pocket money. Pick established apps , and drop any that make withdrawals difficult or push you to deposit money. 5. Online Surveys and Micro-Tasks Estimated earning: ₹500–₹2,500 per month. Ease: very high. Survey panels and micro-task platforms pay for opinions, data labelling, and short tasks. Zero skill needed, works in dead time, pays honestly but modestly. Expect disqualifications from some surveys — your profile will not match every study. Good first rupee online; bad career plan. 6. Reselling with Meesho and WhatsApp Estimated earning: ₹3,000–₹20,000 per month. Ease: high — no inventory, no investment. Reselling apps let you share catalogue products — clothing, home items, accessories — with your own margin added; the platform handles delivery and payment. Your customers are your WhatsApp contacts and social circles, which makes this one of the easiest businesses for homemakers and anyone with an active network. Earnings track how consistently you share and how well you know your audience's taste. 7. Content Creation: YouTube Shorts and Instagram Estimated earning: ₹0 for months, then ₹5,000–₹1,00,000+ once it works. Ease: easy to start, hard to sustain. Short-form content is the highest-ceiling option on this list — and the least predictable. Monetisation comes from ads, brand deals, and affiliate links once you build an audience in a niche you genuinely know. Be honest with yourself: this is a 6–12 month build with no guaranteed payout, best run alongside a steadier earner from this list rather than instead of one. 8. Selling Digital Products (Notes, Templates, Designs) Estimated earning: ₹2,000–₹30,000 per month. Ease: medium — work once, sell forever. Study notes, resume templates, spreadsheet trackers, Canva designs, and mini-courses can be created once and sold repeatedly on marketplaces or through your own social channels. This is the closest thing to passive income on this list that does not require capital — the effort is front-loaded into making something genuinely useful. 9. Website and App Testing Estimated earning: ₹2,000–₹8,000 per month at ₹300–₹1,000 per test. Ease: high. Companies pay real users to try their websites and apps while thinking aloud. Tests take 15–20 minutes with a mic and screen recorder; clear spoken English and a quiet room are the main requirements. Invites are irregular, so treat it as a solid supplement rather than a mainstay. 10. Virtual Assistant and Data Entry Work Estimated earning: ₹8,000–₹25,000 per month. Ease: medium — needs reliability more than talent. Small businesses and busy professionals pay for inbox management, scheduling, research, and data work. The bar is basic computer skills, good communication, and being dependable. Find roles on LinkedIn, Indeed, and freelancing platforms. It is steady, resume-friendly work — and a common stepping stone into operations and admin careers. Which Easy Method Should You Choose? Want the best overall? GroMo — easiest start-to-earning ratio, highest ceiling, zero investment, and it teaches you finance while paying you. Have a skill already? Freelancing or tutoring — highest pay per hour of anything here. Want zero-skill, instant start? Cashback apps, surveys, and testing — real but small money; use them while you build one of the bigger options. Have a strong network? GroMo plus reselling — both monetise trust you already have. Playing the long game? Content creation or digital products — slowest start, biggest possible payoff. The honest pattern across all ten: the truly easy part is starting — every option here can begin today with just your phone and no investment . What separates earners is 90 days of consistency on one method instead of nine days on ten methods. Pick the one that matches your skill and network, ignore anything promising instant riches, and let the first small payout prove to you that online income is real. If you are 18 or older and want the option with the best effort-to-earning ratio, download GroMo , finish the free training, and earn your first commission from the network you already have. FAQ: Easy Ways to Make Money Online What is the easiest way to get money online in India? Cashback apps, online surveys, and micro-task platforms are the easiest — they need no skill and pay real but small amounts (Rs 500-3,000 per month). For meaningful income with an equally easy start, GroMo lets you earn Rs 5,000-50,000+ per month by sharing financial products with their network, with zero investment. Which are the best easy money making apps in India? Stick to apps run by verifiable companies that are free to join and pay to your bank or UPI on a clear schedule. GroMo (financial product commissions), established cashback and rewards apps, reselling apps like Meesho, and reputable survey panels all qualify. Avoid any app that requires a deposit, recharge, or recruiting friends with money — those are scam structures. What are the best ways to make money on the internet without investment? All ten methods in this guide work with zero investment: GroMo, freelancing, tutoring, cashback apps, surveys, reselling, content creation, digital products, website testing, and virtual assistant work. The best pick depends on you — GroMo for the strongest effort-to-earning ratio, freelancing or tutoring if you have a skill, and surveys or cashback if you just want the easiest start. How much money can I realistically make online per month? Zero-skill options pay Rs 500-3,000 per month. Skill-based work — tutoring, freelancing, virtual assistance — typically pays Rs 5,000-25,000 part-time. Network-based earning through GroMo or reselling ranges from Rs 5,000 to Rs 50,000+ per month for consistent users. Most methods pay little in month one and grow substantially by month three to six. How do I avoid online earning scams? Apply three checks: the platform must be free to join, must pay out to your bank or UPI on a published schedule, and must be run by a company you can verify. Walk away instantly from guaranteed returns, pay-to-unlock tasks, deposit-based recruiting, and anyone asking for OTPs. Genuine platforms pay you for work or sales — never for bringing money in. title: The TVR Cerbera Did Everything the Hard Way, Which Makes It Worth Importing
summary: If you were to ever fully understand the world of TVR, Britain’s much-missed sports car underdog, you had to visit Blackpool. The seaside town on Lancashire’s west coast has long been down-at-heel, a poster child for deprivation that feeds off kiss-me-quick tourism like the gulls tussle over fish-and-chip scraps. Employment has been hard to come […]
body_text: If you were to ever fully understand the world of TVR, Britain’s much-missed sports car underdog, you had to visit Blackpool. The seaside town on Lancashire’s west coast has long been down-at-heel, a poster child for deprivation that feeds off kiss-me-quick tourism like the gulls tussle over fish-and-chip scraps. Employment has been hard to come by. Social surveys would regularly highlight how Blackpool held the dubious honor of having more than half of the U.K.’s poorest areas within its footprint. Yet against the odds, the local people were full of fight, their spirit undimmed like the famous (146-years-and-counting) Blackpool Illuminations lights festival. Against this backdrop, TVR was that rare thing: An employer offering the prospect of learning skills, taking home a wage and maybe even having a holiday on a beach somewhere other than Blackpool. Needless to say, jobs at TVR were prized. During the 1990s and 2000s, many of those jobs were in building one of the most interesting (and now importable to the U.S.) performance cars of the era—the Cerbera, named for the three-headed dog in Greek mythology that guards the gates to the underworld. flickr/Alden Jewell The workforce itself was, to put it mildly, charismatic. During one tour while waiting to collect a press car that had been delayed (or was being rebuilt, uncharitable types might say) Ben Samuelson, TVR’s marketing and PR man, told me a tale that illustrated the competitive banter the teams on the two production lines indulged in. Behind the seats of untrimmed fiberglass bodies they would scrawl messages of the sort frequently found inside the lids of old-fashioned school desks. One TVR owner had had all manner of electrical problems with his new pride and joy, and it had been back to the supplying dealer numerous times for repair, only for it to be collected and still have faults. Exasperated, the chap in question insisted that before reassembling the car he come down to the dealer and they show him that everything is in working order. At which point he saw the offensive messages written across the rear bulkhead and, perhaps understandably, suffered a major failure in his sense of humor, which was directed toward company owner Peter Wheeler. But this put Wheeler in something of a predicament, as the workforce weren’t keen to toe the line and end their fun. Instead, they reluctantly agreed to tone down the language and, ahem, illustrations used… The point is, TVR was unlike any other carmaker. Neither traditional like Morgan, nor corporate like Porsche, it was a wild child that did things its own way and didn’t care what anyone said about it, though Wheeler did listen to what dealers and customers said, especially when it came to placing orders. The company couldn’t afford to indulge in costly market research, so through a process of trial and error it would launch new models, first showing them as a concept at a motor show and then weighing up how many deposits came in and whether production was viable or a rethink was needed. TVR Griffith Dean Smith The 1990 concept for the Griffith is a case in point. At the 1990 British Motor Show, TVR showed two cars: the Speed Eight, a 2+2 roadster intended to replace the wedge-era TVRs like the 280i and 400SE; and another concept that brought back the Griffith badge. After the show, Wheeler counted up the deposits. There were 32 for the Speed Eight, and more than 300 for the Griffith. At this point, the company was faithfully following the simple formula that its founder, Trevor Wilkinson, had adopted when he established the firm in 1947: be pragmatic and buy-in all the complicated stuff. Engines came from Rover, Ford, and Triumph, while gearboxes and differentials were off-the-shelf parts. The magic was in how TVR combined those parts with lightweight construction and arresting styling. By the late 1980s, under the ownership of Wheeler, a chemical engineer who struck liquid gold supplying specialist parts to the North Sea oil industry, TVR had found a kind of commercial sweet spot. Cars like the the Griffith made TVR famous for offering near-supercar performance at sports car money. But Wheeler was not content with being seen as a talented assembler of other people’s mechanicals. He wanted TVR to be taken more seriously as a manufacturer. The Cerbera was the manifestation of that ambition. In 1995, Wheeler told Autocar magazine, “You couldn’t have a Ferrari or a Maserati with someone else’s engine in it, could you?” He’d wanted TVR to build its own engines, to both stand apart from peers like Ginetta, Marcos, and Morgan, and to bring more power to the party. The Cerbera would be the first production car to bring the new engines to the road. TVR Chimaera TVR Damian McTaggart takes up the story. The 58-year-old McTaggart was responsible for the exterior design of TVRs, starting with the company in 1989 after one of the strangest job interviews of his career: “Wheeler was in his office with his dog [Ned, a German Pointer] and his dog was sniffing my bollocks while I was doing an interview with him!” The idea for a 2+2 coupe came from Wheeler’s right-hand woman, Dorothy Cureton. As company secretary, she was the trusted filter between TVR dealers and Wheeler, and was said to be at the heart of Wheeler’s closest circle. McTaggart describes Cureton as a powerful figure. “She really did steer the business, I think.” Dealers were telling Cureton they needed another car in the TVR portfolio, something with more than two seats that owners could grow into without losing the brand’s unmistakable character, and Cureton duly convinced Wheeler it was the way to go. McTaggart was tasked with coming up with a concept that could be shown at the 1993 London Motor Show at Earls Court. He remembers it being a frenetic part of his career. “I was so preoccupied with what was going on at Bristol Avenue that I didn’t even bother wearing a watch. I’d go in to work and come home when the task was finished—and if that was the day after, it was the day after,” he laughs. “It’s nuts, but it wasn’t until I left TVR in 2003 that I bought myself a watch. I didn’t need one!” To get started, McTaggart and fellow designer Nick Coughlan scanned a brochure photograph of a Chimaera (a two-seat roadster built by TVR from 1992 to 2003), blew up the side profile and started sketching. The first proposal for the new Cerbera was too short. “I think it was six inches shorter than the production version. You can see that in the first sketch I did.” TVR A full-size prototype was created, which allowed the small team to chop and change to their heart’s content. “I remember taking 20 mm out of the roof [height] one weekend because we just thought the roof looked a bit high. I even remember remodeling the floorpan as well, so if I lowered the roof I could just take a bit more out of the floor and drop the back seats a bit. On the show car, they were separate parts, which lost us a load of space, so when it came to the production version we made the seat back and squab part of the floorpan, with foam straight onto the floor.” McTaggart says working at TVR was both a blessing and a curse. It was a creative, fast-paced environment where decisions were made on the spot. Unfortunately, Wheeler “kept changing his mind” so there was no such thing as a design freeze, from which point a project could be progressed toward production safe in the knowledge there shouldn’t be any fundamental changes. Regardless, the reception from public, press, and dealers alike was overwhelmingly positive: Wheeler reckoned he’d need to gear up the workforce for building 500 Cerberas a year. Then, in 1994, as the concept progressed toward production, a spanner was thrown in the works: BMW bought Rover, and the future looked shaky for the Rover V-8 engine TVR had relied on for so long and was then using in the Griffith and Chimaera. Wheeler decided now was the time to fulfill the long-held ambition and have TVR build its own engines for the Cerbera. By the time the Cerbera went into production for 1996, the doors were 280 mm longer than a Chimaera’s, which helped with access to the back seats, and the wheelbase had grown by six inches. “It also meant we didn’t need a rear quarter light, which means less parts and cost. And it made the car look really fast…” And boy was it fast. With help from the engineers Al Melling and John Ravenscroft, Wheeler created the potent AJP8 (V-8) and, later, AJP6 (straight-six) engines. They were masterpieces of internal-combustion power… when they worked. The all-aluminum AJP8 was said to be as light as contemporary Formula 1 V-8s, helped by a narrow 75-degree angle between cylinder banks (at least 90 degrees is much more common), a flat-plane crank, and a dry sump, as well as a simple two-valve know-how to keep the heads compact and give good torque low in the rev range. There was 320 Ib-ft at 4500 rpm and 350 horsepower at 6500 rpm. It could rev on to 7000 rpm, giving the 2425-pound Cerbera impressive power for the weight. TVR I vividly remember collecting an early Cerbera 4.2 from Blackpool in period for a test drive, and those first few miles on the road. The AJP8 sounded unlike any TVR motor before it, like a superbike on acid, the bassy rumble gone and in its place something altogether race car. It was a loud, purposeful, sharp-edged instrument that soared up and down the rev range with no discernible flywheel effect. The long-travel, floor-hinged throttle had the most wonderful response, and speed would pile on with a voracity that was unlike anything I’d driven before. A Porsche 911 Turbo, Lamborghini Diablo, or Dodge Viper just didn’t feel as fast. Autocar magazine recorded 0–60 mph in 4.0 seconds, 0–100 mph in 9.1 seconds, and a standing quarter-mile in 12.4 seconds. All this from a car that was, at £37,000 (about $57,000), a staggering £20,000 ($30K) cheaper than a Porsche 993 Carrera 2. And it was by far the best-handling TVR to date, too. The longer wheelbase made it more stable and predictable at the limit, the damping was composed, and an integrated roll cage (hidden from sight behind the trim) prevented unruly body flex. It meant you could draw on more of that explosive performance more of the time, especially on Britain’s bumpy back roads, as the Cerbera signaled its intentions and the loaded-up chassis transitioned from grip to slip (more like wild, smoky oversteer) more progressively than any TVR before it, which meant you were better able to put your trust in it. After conducting its first road test of the Cerbera, Autocar concluded the driving experience “gives TVR great cause to be proud” but acknowledged there were still worrying issues around the dependability of the car. I had first-hand experience of those teething problems. When I came to extract a set of performance figures from the car, for Auto Express , a driveshaft broke at the first attempt, despite dropping the clutch at a tentative 2000 rpm in the knowledge that the engine could light up the rear tires without much provocation. “Those driveshafts are the same ones fitted to our Tuscan race cars,” cried the PR man, suggesting I must have been abusing it. Alas, no. Later, its electronically operated door mechanism would lock us out, for no apparent reason, requiring a roadside rescue company to break into the car. A colleague from Top Gear magazine fared worse still, after their test Cerbera locked them inside the car in a hotel car park, at a time when mobile phones were still a rarity. The Cerbera also eschewed modern safety devices such as antilock brakes, traction or stability control, and airbags. Wheeler’s philosophy was that they were an unproven technology, conveniently sidestepping the thorny issue that a little company like TVR couldn’t afford the R&D costs. Wheeler once told PistonHeads : “If someone crashes one of my cars and it’s their fault then I can live with myself. If we were to put an airbag in one of our cars and it ended up killing someone, I couldn’t live with that ”. Hagerty Marketplace Flickr/The Car Spy Yet ensconced in the car’s cockpit, you could almost forgive it its foibles. The Cerbera’s dash layout was the most playful yet from the company, and it represented a dramatic change from the conventional, with buttons for the windscreen wipers, headlights, and horn on the steering wheel, long before Ferrari thought of the idea. The speedo and rev counters sat in a traditional binnacle together with a dial for the water and oil temperature, while below the wheel there was a clock, air vent, fuel gauge and two buttons: a black one to start the engine, and a red one to switch it off. By late 2003, says McTaggart, those early highs of launching the Cerbera were becoming a distant memory. The latest six-cylinder AJP6, aka the “Speed Six,” had been added to the Cerbera range, the Tuscan targa model had arrived, and customer complaints were piling up. “We were having all sorts of problems with the straight-six engines, and it just drained the lifeblood out of the company,” recalls McTaggart. Flickr/The Car Spy “There was never very much profit in any of the cars, and I remember walking across to the service area one day, and there was something like 20 to 30 engines sat there, with their cars all out in the car park with their noses pointing to the sky. That’s not sustainable. They’d come back for one or maybe even two engine rebuilds, and there’s the profit from that car just gone…” McTaggart thinks the idea to have home-grown engines was the wrong strategy. “I think that’s where he [Peter Wheeler] started to go wrong, because he started to rule the company with his heart rather than his head. I mean, a McLaren F1’s got a BMW engine in it and nobody questions it—it’s seen as a good thing. He could have done something similar.” If there was a moment in time when Wheeler’s commitment to the company began to waiver, it was likely in 2000, shortly after deliveries of the new Tuscan began. “We had been having all sorts of engine trouble,” recalls McTaggart, “and the press had been given a Tuscan to road test and the roof blew off, and I remember walking the production line with Peter and he said, ‘I can’t do this anymore’. I kept my mouth shut and didn’t say anything to anybody but started thinking about what I should do next.” Wheeler sold the rights to TVR to Nikolai Smolenski, the son of a Russian oligarch, in 2004, for a reported £15M. By late 2006, the company had gone into receivership. Adam Wilcox Reflecting on the rise of the Cerbera, in 2004 Wheeler admitted to Management Today magazine that it quickly went from being a high point to a low point in the company’s history. “It was a complicated car to make: the first with our own engine, and the trimming was very labour intensive to fit. I decided to man the company up to deal with a rate of 10 orders a week, just to make sure that customers wouldn’t have to wait longer than eighteen months. Because every job is hands on, it takes quite a lot of time to train workers, so it was 100 people—a big expansion of the workforce at that point. But the orders never came in at that rate.” Today, the Cerbera occupies a fascinating place in TVR’s story. It remains astonishingly fast, charismatic, and unapologetically unlike anything else. It was the car that proved TVR could design its own engines, build a genuinely complex modern GT, and compete at the very highest level on its own terms. It was also the car that exposed the limits of that ambition, as complexity, reliability issues, and financial pressures began to mount. TVR never made an attempt to sell the Cerbera, nor any of its cars of the 1990s and 2000s, in the United States. Now comfortably past the 25-year rule for importing foreign-market vehicles, though, it is possible for American enthusiasts to take the plunge and own one of these fascinating cars. Should you dare to import a Cerbera? If you crave one of the most exciting performance cars of the ’90s, don’t hesitate. There are always examples for sale, some good, some bad, and prices range between £20,000 and £40,000 (about $27K to $54K at current exchange rates) in the U.K., depending on whether they’ve been rebuilt or not. A good place to start is Str8six, which often has excellent examples for sale. Values also depend on engine, as the car was available with the Speed Six and the V-8 that came in 4.2-, 4.5-, and 4.7-liter sizes. Prices for the Cerbera are updated in the U.K. version of the Hagerty Price Guide. There are even specialists on hand in the U.S. who import and help maintain modern TVRs, notably TVR Imports and TVR Garage , both in Arizona. On the U.S. side, barely more than a handful of Cerberas have sold publicly, and they’ve brought prices in the $40,000–$50,000 range. A lot of car for the money, but there are some caveats, of course. Needless to say, a Cerbera is a purchase you make with your eyes wide open, ideally with the reassurance of an inspection by a trusted specialist who knows these cars inside out. Once you have a Cerbera, parts won’t be easy to source, and problems won’t be easy to diagnose. But it will look, sound, and drive unlike anything else on an American road. For an all-too short and thrilling time, Wheeler and TVR made Blackpool as famous for its cars as anything else. And of the lot, the Cerbera really did shine brightest. title: What's New in Vesence: July 2026
summary: July went into the web app: in-browser editors for every surface an agent touches, Vesence Projects, a Library of apps your own firm builds, a task and chat hierarchy for dividing complex work, and integrations with virtually any third-party system.
body_text: The Web App Almost everything we shipped in July points in one direction: the web app. Vesence began as an intelligence layer inside Microsoft Office, and Word, Outlook, Excel, and PowerPoint are still where the work gets finished. But the place people direct that work from has become the web. So July went into building the most powerful agentic workspace on the market: one intuitive place to brief agents, watch them work, and take over the moment you want to. Five things stand out. 1. Create and Edit Directly in the Web You can now create and manually edit emails, Teams messages, documents, spreadsheets, and PowerPoint presentations directly within the chat. Each surface has a real editor rather than a preview, so changing a sentence no longer means downloading a file. Everything an agent proposes arrives as tracked changes. Step through them, accept, reject, or type over them yourself, and the formatting holds throughout. More in Introducing Vesence Editor . 2. Vesence Projects Most professional work isn't a single question. It's a matter that runs for weeks around the same files, the same colleagues, and the same standing instructions. Projects give that work a home: files, chats, and drafts in one place, shared with your team. Data, files, context, and instructions live on the project, and every chat inside it inherits them, so users and agents can work continuously around the same matter instead of restarting each session. It's an addition to SharePoint or your DMS, not a replacement. More in Introducing Vesence Projects . 3. A New Task and Chat Hierarchy A task can now contain multiple chats. Complex work divides into separate conversations that stay organized under the same objective — one chat drafting the agreement, another checking cross-references, a third working through the counterparty's comments. This is structure more than it is a feature, and it's what makes long-running work across many agents legible. You can see what's running, what finished, and what still needs you. 4. An App Store for Every Organization Users can build their own apps in Vesence and share them across the organization. Describe the tool your team needs and the agent builds it: a chronology tracker, a cap table reconciler, a conditions precedent monitor. Publish an app to your firm's Library and it appears in everyone's launchpad. In effect, each organization ends up with a private app store tailored to its own processes, built by the people who actually know the work. More in Introducing Vesence Apps . 5. Custom CLIs and Third-Party Integrations Organizations can now integrate virtually any third-party system into Vesence: ERP systems, timekeeping tools, document templating software, and accounting platforms. It works through custom CLIs. Rather than a bespoke connector per system, agents get a command-line interface to yours — the same mechanism they already use to read and write Office files. Adding a system becomes a matter of describing it. What This Adds Up To Taken together, July moves Vesence past being an AI chat interface. People, agents, data, applications, and enterprise systems now work together in one place: you direct the work, and it gets done in the tools you already use. Also shipped this month: Vesence Compare for end-to-end document comparison, and bulk email generation . Getting Started Everything above is available today. Book a demo or start a free trial .

title: 10 delicious ways to enjoy Alvalle gazpacho this summer
summary: Whether you're new to gazpacho or searching for creative ways to serve it, PepsiCo’s Alvalle gazpacho is a ready-to-eat option that can be incorporated into lunches, small dinners, entertaining, and everyday moments.
body_text: Summer is the perfect time to enjoy refreshing dishes that don't require extra preparation. That's one reason gazpacho — a chilled soup made with real vegetables — has been a staple of Mediterranean tables for generations. Originating in Spain and loved across Western Europe, where gazpacho is a beloved culinary tradition, Alvalle Gazpacho is now available in the U.S. at select Whole Foods Market stores. It brings that tradition to modern consumers looking for convenient foods made with recognizable ingredients. Crafted with real vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, onions and garlic, along with extra virgin olive oil, and kept refrigerated to preserve its fresh taste, Alvalle is ready whenever you are — whether you're looking for an easy addition to a quick lunch, a small dinner, or your next gathering. "Today’s consumers want foods that are flavorful and convenient, without having to compromise on quality or taste," said Marisa Perez, senior vice president and general manager, Fresh Experiences Portfolio at PepsiCo Foods U.S. "Alvalle brings the vibrant flavors of the Mediterranean to life with high-quality ingredients in a ready-to-enjoy format, making it easy to enjoy as part of from a small lunch to an afternoon pick-me-up and everything in between." One of the things that makes gazpacho unique is its versatility. While traditionally enjoyed as a chilled soup, it can also be served as an appetizer, paired with sandwiches and salads, enjoyed alongside grilled meals, or even sipped straight from a glass.

title: Operações Inteligentes ajudam os varejistas a serem melhores todos os dias
summary: Com as expectativas dos consumidores mudando, os varejistas enfrentam um ponto de virada. A necessidade urgente de maior eficiência e adaptabilidade significa que os varejistas devem evoluir e melhorar a satisfação do cliente todos os dias, além de atender às demandas crescentes. A pesquisa que divulgamos recentemente com a Oxford Economics lança luz sobre como as operações inteligentes podem transformar o setor do varejo.

A necessidade urgente de maior eficiência e adaptabilidade significa que os varejistas devem evoluir e melhorar a satisfação do cliente todos os dias, além de atender às demandas crescentes. A pesquisa que divulgamos recentemente com a Oxford Economics lança luz sobre como as operações inteligentes podem transformar o setor do varejo. Ao adotar tecnologias que fornecem insights em tempo real, promovem a colaboração conectada e integram a automação, os varejistas podem adaptar uma mentalidade de melhoria contínua, construir um crescimento sustentável e permanecer competitivos em um cenário em constante mudança. Operações inteligentes abrem o caminho para o futuro A inteligência operacional tornou-se um elemento crítico para os varejistas que buscam prosperar. O estudo destaca que as organizações que investem em operações inteligentes, impulsionadas por IA, automação e análise avançada de dados, alcançam ganhos significativos em lucratividade, satisfação do cliente e produtividade dos funcionários. Por exemplo, as empresas que introduziram melhorias significativas no fluxo de trabalho tiveram uma média de 1,8% a mais de crescimento da receita e 1,5% a mais de lucratividade no último ano. O conceito de "operações inteligentes" representa uma mudança em relação a fluxos de trabalho desatualizados e sistemas isolados. Envolve a criação de ambientes onde os dados fluem de forma integrada, permitindo a tomada de decisões informadas com agilidade e precisão. Ferramentas como leitores RFID , computadores móveis e software de análise preditiva estão se mostrando essenciais para otimizar o gerenciamento de inventário, que continua sendo uma prioridade para 39% dos varejistas pesquisados. Combine tecnologia e expertise humana O estudo enfatiza a importância de combinar avanços tecnológicos com a expertise dos funcionários da linha de frente. Ferramentas de automação, como previsão de demanda e otimização de estoque orientadas por IA, reduzem tarefas repetitivas, permitindo que os funcionários se concentrem mais no engajamento com o cliente. Essa abordagem aumenta a eficiência operacional e apoia a satisfação dos funcionários, o que é um fator vital para reter pessoal qualificado no mercado de trabalho competitivo de hoje. Por exemplo, a integração de dispositivos móveis e IA permite que os funcionários acessem dados de estoque em tempo real, melhorando tanto a velocidade quanto a precisão. Um líder da cadeia de suprimentos observou como equipar os funcionários com Tablets e Software avançado transformou suas operações, afirmando: "A melhor coisa que aconteceu para nós...é que atualizamos a tecnologia e colocamos nas mãos dos próprios colaboradores." Dados, a base da transformação do varejo Os dados estão no centro das operações inteligentes. No entanto, o estudo revela que quase dois terços dos varejistas enfrentam desafios com sistemas isolados e capacidades limitadas de análise de dados. Para resolver isso, os varejistas devem adotar sistemas robustos de gestão de dados que ofereçam insights em tempo real e análises preditivas. Esses sistemas impulsionam a eficiência operacional e elevam a experiência do cliente, garantindo que os produtos estejam disponíveis quando e onde são necessários. A estrutura da Modern Store da Zebra exemplifica essa abordagem, integrando soluções de captura de dados com fluxos de trabalho inteligentes para gerar insights acionáveis. Ao aproveitar ferramentas como prateleiras inteligentes, etiquetas RFID e análises com tecnologia de IA , os varejistas alcançam maior precisão no inventário e reduzem os desafios de prevenção de perdas. Essas melhorias impactam diretamente a lucratividade e promovem a fidelidade do cliente. O futuro do varejo é digitalizado e automatizado, com Linhas de frente conectadas A Zebra Technologies visualiza um futuro onde as operações de linha de frente estão totalmente digitalizadas e otimizadas. Essa visão decorre da crença de que a tecnologia deve capacitar as pessoas, melhorando o trabalho todos os dias para os funcionários e os clientes que eles atendem. Ao promover uma cultura de inovação e melhoria contínua, a Zebra permite que os varejistas se adaptem às mudanças nas condições de mercado e às expectativas dos clientes em evolução. Nosso estudo reforça essa visão, mostrando que a otimização do fluxo de trabalho ajuda as organizações a alcançar melhores resultados financeiros, ao mesmo tempo em que constroem relações mais fortes com clientes e funcionários. Por exemplo, varejistas que melhoraram seus fluxos de trabalho de prevenção de perdas experimentaram um aumento de 1,2% no crescimento da receita, agregando valor significativo aos seus negócios. Faça parceria com a Zebra para Operações Inteligentes Junto com nossos parceiros e clientes, estamos moldando um futuro onde as operações são eficientes, inteligentes e centradas nas necessidades humanas. O momento de começar essa transformação é agora — porque o melhor começa hoje. Como líder global em operações inteligentes, a Zebra Technologies está posicionada de forma única para ajudar os varejistas a navegar nessa transformação. Com décadas de experiência em captura de dados e automação, a Zebra oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções projetadas para conectar a linha de frente, melhorar a visibilidade e otimizar fluxos de trabalho. A gestão de inventário com tecnologia de IA e a priorização de tarefas em tempo real são apenas algumas das ferramentas que a Zebra oferece para ajudar os varejistas a alcançar seus objetivos operacionais com precisão e confiança. A dedicação da Zebra à inovação e ao sucesso do cliente é evidente em suas relações, incluindo nossa colaboração com a Oxford Economics. Esta aliança fornece insights valiosos sobre as tendências do setor e posiciona a Zebra como um consultor confiável para os líderes de varejo em todo o mundo. As descobertas do nosso estudo destacam a necessidade crítica de operações inteligentes no setor de varejo. Ao adotar tecnologias que fornecem insights em tempo real, promovem a colaboração conectada e integram a automação, os varejistas estão descobrindo oportunidades notáveis para inovar e se destacar em um ambiente competitivo.
